lessons.title: Introduction
body: An Android app is not one long-running program. The system starts and stops its **components** (Activities, Services, BroadcastReceivers and ContentProviders) whenever it needs to, and it can kill your whole process at any time to free memory.
Interviewers test whether you design for this: state that survives rotation and process death, work that keeps going when the screen goes away, and no leaks of a dead `Context`.
points: The four app components and what each is for
The system, not you, owns the lifecycle
Process death is normal, not an edge case
lessons.tip: When asked "what happens when the user rotates the phone?", answer in three parts: the Activity is destroyed and recreated, ViewModel survives, and savedInstanceState covers process death.

code.title: The four components in the manifest
code.src:
<application android:name=".App">
    <activity android:name=".MainActivity" android:exported="true">
        <intent-filter>
            <action android:name="android.intent.action.MAIN" />
            <category android:name="android.intent.category.LAUNCHER" />
        </intent-filter>
    </activity>
    <service android:name=".PlayerService" android:foregroundServiceType="mediaPlayback" />
    <receiver android:name=".BootReceiver" android:exported="false" />
    <provider android:name=".FilesProvider" android:authorities="io.app.files" />
</application>

p: Every app runs in its own Linux process with its own instance of the Android Runtime (ART). The process is forked from **Zygote**, a pre-warmed process that already has the framework classes loaded, which is why apps start faster than a plain JVM would.

Your code never calls `main()`. The system talks to your process through **Binder** (Android's inter-process communication) and tells the `ActivityThread` to create components. Every lifecycle callback you write is the system calling into your code on the **main thread**, which runs a `Looper` that processes one message at a time.

That single main thread draws the UI, handles input and runs lifecycle callbacks. If you block it for about 5 seconds while handling input, the system shows an **ANR** (Application Not Responding) dialog.

deep.h: Process priority and why your app gets killed
p: Android ranks processes by importance: **foreground** (visible Activity the user is using, or a foreground service), **visible**, **service**, and **cached** (nothing visible). When memory runs low, the low-memory killer removes cached processes first.

Your app is killed silently with no `onDestroy` call. When the user returns, Android recreates the Activity and hands it the `Bundle` saved earlier, so the user should see the same screen as if nothing happened. This is why saved state matters.

`Context` is your handle to the system: resources, files, preferences, starting components. **Application context** lives as long as the process. **Activity context** also carries the theme and window, and dies with the Activity.

Rule of thumb: use the Activity context for anything UI-related (inflating views, dialogs, themed resources), and the Application context for anything that outlives a screen (singletons, databases, WorkManager).

code.title: Picking the right Context

mistakes.bad: Keeping an Activity in a static field or singleton
mistakes.good: Store `context.applicationContext`, or pass the Context per call.

mistakes.bad: Assuming `onDestroy` always runs
mistakes.good: Save important data as it changes; the process can die without callbacks.

mistakes.bad: Doing disk or network work in `onCreate` on the main thread
mistakes.good: Move it to a coroutine on `Dispatchers.IO`, triggered from the ViewModel.

qa.q: What happens, step by step, when the user taps your app icon and the process is not running?
qa.a: The launcher sends an Intent to the system (ActivityManagerService). Since there is no process, Zygote forks a new one. In it, ActivityThread starts, creates the Application object and calls `Application.onCreate`. Then the launcher Activity is created and moved through `onCreate`, `onStart` and `onResume`, and the first frame is drawn. That is a **cold start**; heavy work in `Application.onCreate` delays all of it.

lessons.title: Activity lifecycle
body: An Activity moves through `onCreate` → `onStart` → `onResume` when it comes to the front, and `onPause` → `onStop` → `onDestroy` as it leaves. **Started** means visible, **resumed** means it has focus and takes input.

A configuration change (rotation, dark mode, language) destroys and recreates the Activity. Pressing Home only stops it. The process can then be killed while stopped, and the user returns to a fresh Activity that receives the saved `Bundle`.
points: onCreate: inflate UI, restore state, set up observers
onStart/onStop: visible or not; start and stop UI work here
onResume/onPause: foreground focus; keep it fast
isChangingConfigurations tells rotation apart from finishing
onSaveInstanceState runs before the Activity may be killed
lessons.tip: Know the order when Activity A starts Activity B: A.onPause → B.onCreate → B.onStart → B.onResume → A.onStop. It is a very common trick question.

code.title: Lifecycle-aware collection instead of manual start and stop

deep.h: What the lifecycle states really mean
p: The lifecycle is a **state machine**: INITIALIZED → CREATED → STARTED → RESUMED, and back down to DESTROYED. Callbacks are the transitions between states. Jetpack exposes the state as `lifecycle.currentState`, so components can react to it without the Activity forwarding every callback.

STARTED means the window is visible, possibly behind a dialog or in multi-window. RESUMED means it is the focused, interactive Activity. In multi-window mode several Activities can be STARTED, but only the top focused one is RESUMED (since Android 10, all visible ones can be resumed, with one holding top focus).

On rotation the system calls `onPause`, `onStop`, `onSaveInstanceState`, `onDestroy` on the old instance and then creates a brand-new instance with `onCreate(savedInstanceState)`. The new instance gets new views and new resources for the new configuration.

The `ViewModelStore` is retained across this recreation (via the non-configuration instance), so the same ViewModel object is handed to the new Activity. That is why a ViewModel survives rotation but not process death: process death destroys the store too.

You can opt out with `android:configChanges` and handle the change yourself in `onConfigurationChanged`. That is fine for things like a video player, but it is easy to get wrong because resources do not reload automatically.

`onSaveInstanceState` writes to a `Bundle` that the system keeps outside your process. It must be small (the whole transaction is limited to about 1 MB, shared with other data), so save IDs and user input, not lists or bitmaps. Views with an `id` save some of their own state automatically, such as EditText text and scroll positions.

code.title: What survives what

mistakes.bad: Starting location updates in `onCreate` and never stopping them
mistakes.good: Tie them to STARTED with `repeatOnLifecycle` or a lifecycle-aware observer.

mistakes.bad: Putting a large list into the saved Bundle
mistakes.good: Save an ID or query; reload the data from the repository.

mistakes.bad: Using `configChanges` to "fix" rotation bugs
mistakes.good: Fix the state handling instead; process death will still expose the same bug.

qa.q: What is the difference between ViewModel and onSaveInstanceState? When do you need both?
qa.a: ViewModel keeps any amount of in-memory data across configuration changes, but is lost on process death. `onSaveInstanceState` (or SavedStateHandle) survives process death but only holds small, serialisable data. In practice you use both: the ViewModel holds the loaded data, and SavedStateHandle holds the minimum needed to reload it, such as the selected ID and the search query.

lessons.title: Fragments and their two lifecycles
body: A Fragment has its own lifecycle **and** a separate view lifecycle. On the back stack, the Fragment object stays alive while its view is destroyed (`onDestroyView`) and later recreated.
That is why you observe with `viewLifecycleOwner` and clear the view binding in `onDestroyView`. Otherwise you leak a whole view tree, or receive duplicate observers each time the view comes back.
points: Communicate through a shared ViewModel or the Fragment Result API, not direct references
FragmentManager back stack and commit vs commitNow
lessons.tip: If an interviewer asks about a memory leak in a Fragment, the binding held past onDestroyView is the first thing to mention.

code.title: Safe view binding in a Fragment

deep.h: Why a Fragment has two lifecycles
p: A Fragment can exist without a view. When you navigate forward and the Fragment goes onto the back stack, FragmentManager destroys its **view** to save memory but keeps the Fragment **instance** with its fields. When you press Back, `onCreateView` runs again on the same instance.

So anything tied to views (bindings, adapters holding views, observers that update views) must follow the **view lifecycle**, while things tied to the Fragment itself (arguments, ViewModels) follow the Fragment lifecycle.

`commit()` schedules the transaction on the main thread's queue; it does not run immediately. `commitNow()` runs it synchronously but cannot be added to the back stack. `commitAllowingStateLoss()` lets it run after `onSaveInstanceState`, accepting that the change may be lost on process death.

Committing after state is saved throws `IllegalStateException: Can not perform this action after onSaveInstanceState`. This often happens when a network callback arrives while the app is in the background; collecting with `repeatOnLifecycle` avoids it because the UI only reacts while STARTED.

Fragments should not hold references to each other. Use an **Activity-scoped shared ViewModel** (`activityViewModels()`) for shared state, or the **Fragment Result API** for one-off results such as a picker returning a value.

code.title: Fragment Result API

mistakes.bad: Observing with `this` instead of `viewLifecycleOwner` in a Fragment
mistakes.good: Observers pile up each time the view is recreated; use `viewLifecycleOwner`.

mistakes.bad: Passing data through a Fragment constructor
mistakes.good: Use `arguments` (a Bundle); the system recreates Fragments with the empty constructor.

mistakes.bad: Calling `commit()` from a background callback
mistakes.good: Collect results while STARTED, so transactions only happen when state is not saved.

qa.q: Why does Android require Fragments to have an empty constructor?
qa.a: After a configuration change or process death, FragmentManager recreates Fragments by reflection using the no-argument constructor, then restores their `arguments` Bundle. Any values passed through a custom constructor would be lost. Put input data in `arguments` (or navigation args) and, for dependencies, use a FragmentFactory or Hilt.

lessons.title: Intents, tasks and launch modes
body: An **explicit** Intent names the component to start; an **implicit** Intent describes an action (`ACTION_VIEW`, `ACTION_SEND`) and the system finds an app that matches an intent filter. Since Android 12, any component with an intent filter must declare `android:exported`.

Activities live in **tasks** (back stacks). Launch modes and flags such as `singleTop`, `singleTask` and `FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP` control whether a new instance is created or an existing one receives `onNewIntent`.
points: PendingIntent lets another app (e.g. notifications) start your component; choose FLAG_IMMUTABLE by default
lessons.tip: Mention that PendingIntents should be FLAG_IMMUTABLE unless something must fill in extras; it is a security question disguised as an API question.

code.title: Handling a deep link that may arrive twice

deep.h: How the system resolves an implicit Intent
p: For an implicit Intent, PackageManager compares its **action**, **categories** and **data** (scheme, host, path, MIME type) against every registered intent filter. All three tests must pass. If several apps match, the user sees a chooser (or the default app for that link).
From Android 11, **package visibility** limits which other apps you can see. To query or launch a specific app you must declare it in a `<queries>` element in the manifest.

A **task** is a stack of Activities the user sees as one unit in Recents. `standard` always creates a new instance on top. `singleTop` reuses the instance only if it is already on top (it receives `onNewIntent`). `singleTask` keeps one instance in its task and clears everything above it when relaunched. `singleInstance` puts the Activity alone in its own task.

Flags do similar things per launch: `FLAG_ACTIVITY_NEW_TASK` (required when starting from a non-Activity context), `FLAG_ACTIVITY_CLEAR_TOP` (pop everything above an existing instance) and `FLAG_ACTIVITY_SINGLE_TOP`.

A **deep link** is any URI your app handles via an intent filter; the user may get a chooser. An **Android App Link** is an `https` link verified with a `assetlinks.json` file on your domain, so it opens your app directly without a chooser.

code.title: A verified App Link filter
code.src:
<intent-filter android:autoVerify="true">
    <action android:name="android.intent.action.VIEW" />
    <category android:name="android.intent.category.DEFAULT" />
    <category android:name="android.intent.category.BROWSABLE" />
    <data android:scheme="https" android:host="droidly.io" android:pathPrefix="/q/" />
</intent-filter>

mistakes.bad: Forgetting `android:exported` on components with intent filters (crash on install from Android 12)
mistakes.good: Declare it explicitly; use `false` unless other apps must start it.

mistakes.bad: Using mutable PendingIntents by default
mistakes.good: Use `FLAG_IMMUTABLE`; only use `FLAG_MUTABLE` when another app must fill in data.

mistakes.bad: Using `singleTask` to prevent duplicate screens
mistakes.good: Usually `singleTop` or proper navigation is the right fix; `singleTask` changes back-stack behaviour in surprising ways.

qa.q: A notification opens a details screen. When the user presses Back, they leave the app instead of going to the home screen. How do you fix it?
qa.a: Build a proper back stack for the notification. Use `TaskStackBuilder` (or the Navigation component's `NavDeepLinkBuilder`) so the PendingIntent starts the home Activity with the details Activity on top. Then Back goes to home, as the user expects.

lessons.title: Services, background work and process death
body: A **foreground service** shows a notification and is for work the user is aware of right now: music, navigation, an active call. Modern Android heavily restricts background services, so deferrable work belongs in **WorkManager**, which survives reboots and respects battery constraints.

For UI state, use **ViewModel** for rotation and **SavedStateHandle** (backed by the saved Bundle) for process death. Keep only small, essential state there, such as IDs and scroll position, not whole lists.
points: Foreground service vs WorkManager vs coroutine in a ViewModel
Process death: how to test it ("Don't keep activities", or adb shell am kill)
lessons.tip: Ask yourself "what if the process dies here?" out loud during design questions. It signals real production experience.

code.title: Surviving process death with SavedStateHandle

deep.h: Choosing the right tool for background work
p: Ask two questions: **must it run now** (while the user waits), and **must it finish** even if the user leaves? Work tied to a screen goes in `viewModelScope`. Work that must finish but can be deferred goes to **WorkManager**, which persists the request in a database and runs it under constraints, even after a reboot.

User-visible ongoing work (music, navigation, an active upload the user started) uses a **foreground service** with a notification and, from Android 14, a declared `foregroundServiceType`. Exact alarms for alarm-clock apps use AlarmManager.

deep.h: How WorkManager works under the hood
p: WorkManager stores each request in its own Room database, then schedules it using JobScheduler (API 23+). When constraints are met, it runs your `Worker` or `CoroutineWorker`. It retries with backoff when you return `Result.retry()`, and supports unique work, chaining and periodic work (minimum 15-minute interval).
Because requests are persisted, they survive process death and reboots. That is the main difference from a coroutine, which dies with the process.

Rotation does not test process death. To test it: put the app in the background, then run `adb shell am kill <package>` (kills only background processes), and reopen it from Recents. Or enable **Don't keep activities** in Developer options to test Activity recreation.

code.title: Background work decision guide

mistakes.bad: Using a background `Service` for uploads
mistakes.good: Background service starts are restricted from Android 8; use WorkManager or a foreground service.

mistakes.bad: Launching long work in `GlobalScope` from an Activity
mistakes.good: Use WorkManager if it must finish; otherwise use `viewModelScope`.

mistakes.bad: Testing only rotation and calling it "state handling done"
mistakes.good: Also test process death with `adb shell am kill`.

qa.q: How would you upload a large video so it completes even if the user closes the app?
qa.a: Use WorkManager with a network constraint and an expedited or long-running `CoroutineWorker`. Call `setForeground` to show progress in a notification, since long uploads run as a foreground service under the hood. Upload in chunks with a resumable protocol, so a retry continues from the last confirmed chunk instead of starting over. Use unique work keyed by the video ID to avoid duplicates.

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Kotlin interviews rarely ask you to recite syntax. They check whether you use the type system to make bugs impossible: nullability, immutable data, exhaustive `when`, and small functions that compose.
Expect questions that compare features (`val` vs `const`, `data` vs regular class, `let` vs `apply`) and "what does this compile to" questions about `inline`, `object` and extension functions.
lessons.tip: Write answers in idiomatic Kotlin even on a whiteboard: expression bodies, immutable vals and the elvis operator read as fluency.

code.title: Idiomatic Kotlin in a few lines

deep.h: Why Kotlin feels different from Java
p: Kotlin moves many runtime failures to compile time. Nullability is part of the type, `when` can be checked for exhaustiveness, and `val` makes immutability the default. Interviewers look for code that uses these features to make wrong states impossible.

Kotlin compiles to the same JVM bytecode as Java, so features like `data class`, `object` and extension functions are compiler conveniences. Knowing what they compile to helps you answer performance and interop questions.
`if`, `when` and `try` are expressions that return values, so you rarely need temporary `var`s. Functions with a single expression can use `=` instead of a block body.

code.title: Expressions instead of statements

mistakes.bad: Writing Java-style code with `var`s and null checks everywhere
mistakes.good: Prefer `val`, expression bodies and the elvis operator.

mistakes.bad: Using `!!` to silence the compiler
mistakes.good: Handle the null case or change the type so null cannot occur.

qa.q: What does a Kotlin `object` declaration compile to?
qa.a: A class with a private constructor and a static `INSTANCE` field initialised in a static block. Initialisation is lazy (on first access of the class) and thread-safe, because the JVM guarantees class initialisation happens once. From Java you access it as `MyObject.INSTANCE`, unless members are marked `@JvmStatic`.

lessons.title: Null safety
body: Every type is either nullable (`String?`) or not (`String`), and the compiler forces you to handle null before use. Use `?.` for safe calls, `?:` for a default, and smart casts after a null check.

`!!` throws a NullPointerException and should be rare. `lateinit` is for non-null properties set after construction (e.g. by DI); `by lazy` computes once on first access and is thread-safe by default.
points: Smart casts after checks (only on stable values)
lessons.tip: Platform types from Java are the hidden source of NPEs in Kotlin code. Mention annotating Java APIs with @Nullable/@NonNull.

code.title: lateinit vs lazy

deep.h: How null safety works at runtime
p: Nullability is mostly a compile-time feature. The compiler inserts checks only at the boundaries: when a public function takes a non-null parameter, Kotlin adds `Intrinsics.checkNotNullParameter` so Java callers cannot pass null unnoticed.

Values coming from Java have **platform types** (shown as `String!`). The compiler lets you treat them as nullable or not, and if you guess wrong you get a NullPointerException. Annotating Java code with `@Nullable`/`@NonNull` turns these into real Kotlin types.

After `if (x != null)` or `if (x is String)`, the compiler treats `x` as the narrower type, but only if it can prove `x` cannot change in between. Local `val`s and `val` properties without custom getters in the same module qualify. A `var` property can be changed by another thread, so it is not smart cast; copy it into a local `val` first.

code.title: Smart cast on a var property

p: `lateinit var` has no initial value and throws `UninitializedPropertyAccessException` if read too early. It only works on non-primitive `var`s, and you can check `::prop.isInitialized`. `by lazy` is for `val`s; the first read runs the initialiser and caches the result. The default mode is synchronized; use `LazyThreadSafetyMode.NONE` on the main thread to avoid locking.

mistakes.bad: Reading a `lateinit` property before it is set
mistakes.good: Initialise it in `onCreate`/DI, or use a nullable type or `lazy`.

mistakes.bad: Trusting Java return values to be non-null
mistakes.good: Treat platform types as nullable unless the Java API is annotated.

mistakes.bad: Chaining `?.let { }` five levels deep
mistakes.good: Use early returns with `?: return` for readable code.

qa.q: What is the difference between `?.let { }` and `if (x != null)`?
qa.a: Both handle null, but `?.let` works on any expression (including mutable properties) because it captures the value once into `it`, while `if (x != null)` only smart-casts stable values. `?.let` also returns the lambda result, so you can chain `?:` for a default. For multiple statements, an early `val v = x ?: return` is often the most readable.

lessons.title: Data, sealed and value classes
body: A **data class** generates `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString`, `copy` and `componentN` from the primary constructor. Only primary-constructor properties take part in equality.

A **sealed** class or interface restricts its subclasses to the same module and package, so `when` can be exhaustive with no `else`. That makes it perfect for UI state and results. A **value class** wraps one value with no allocation at runtime, giving type safety for IDs.
points: Sealed hierarchies for state and events
object for singletons, data object for sealed leaves
lessons.tip: When you add a new state, an exhaustive when turns a runtime bug into a compile error. Say exactly that in the interview.

code.title: Modelling screen state

p: For each property in the primary constructor, a data class generates `componentN()` (for destructuring), plus `equals`, `hashCode`, `toString` and `copy`. Properties declared in the class body are ignored by all of these, which is a common source of surprising equality bugs.
`copy()` is a **shallow** copy. If a property is a mutable list, both copies share it. Prefer immutable collections in data classes so `copy` is safe.

An enum has a fixed set of **instances**, all of the same shape. A sealed class has a fixed set of **subclasses**, each with its own data. Use an enum for simple choices (`Theme.DARK`), and a sealed type when cases carry different data (`Loaded(items)` vs `Error(message)`).
Because the compiler knows every subclass, `when` over a sealed type is exhaustive. Adding a new subclass breaks every `when` that does not handle it, at compile time.

`@JvmInline value class UserId(val raw: String)` is a separate type at compile time, so you cannot pass an `OrderId` where a `UserId` is expected. At runtime it is usually just the `String`, with no wrapper object. It gets boxed when used as a generic type or a nullable type.

code.title: Data class equality pitfall

mistakes.bad: Declaring important fields in the data class body
mistakes.good: Put every field that defines the value in the primary constructor.

mistakes.bad: Using `var` and mutable lists inside UI state data classes
mistakes.good: Use `val` and read-only `List`; update with `copy`.

mistakes.bad: Using a sealed class with an `else` branch in `when`
mistakes.good: Drop `else` so the compiler flags new cases.

qa.q: Why should UI state classes be immutable?
qa.a: Immutable state can be compared and shared safely. StateFlow and Compose decide whether to update by comparing old and new values; if you mutate a list inside the same object, the reference is equal and the UI does not update. Immutability also removes threading bugs, because no one can change the object after it is published. You create a new state with `copy`.

lessons.title: Scope functions and extensions
body: `let`, `run`, `with`, `apply` and `also` differ in two ways: how they refer to the object (`it` or `this`) and what they return (the lambda result or the object itself).
Extension functions add functions to a type without inheritance. They are resolved **statically** from the declared type, so they cannot be overridden and cannot access private members.
points: apply: configure an object, returns it
let: transform or null-check, returns result
run / with: compute with this, returns result
lessons.tip: Overusing nested scope functions hurts readability. Interviewers like hearing "I keep them one level deep."

code.title: Choosing the right scope function
code.src:
val request = Request.Builder().apply {      // configure, returns the builder
    url(endpoint)
    header("Authorization", "Bearer $token")
}.build()

val user = repo.find(id)
    ?.also { log("found ${it.id}") }         // side effect, keeps the value
    ?.let { it.copy(name = it.name.trim()) } // transform

fun View.show(visible: Boolean) { isVisible = visible }   // extension

deep.h: The two questions that pick a scope function
p: 1) Do you want to refer to the object as `this` (configuring it) or `it` (passing it around)? 2) Do you want to get the **object back** or the **lambda result**? `apply` = this + object, `also` = it + object, `run`/`with` = this + result, `let` = it + result.
All five are `inline`, so there is no runtime cost. They exist purely for readability, which means overusing them defeats the point.

An extension compiles to a static function whose first parameter is the receiver: `fun View.show()` becomes `static void show(View $this)`. That is why extensions are resolved by the **declared** type at compile time, not by the runtime type, and why a member function always wins over an extension with the same signature.

code.title: Static dispatch of extensions
code.src:
open class Shape
class Circle : Shape()

fun Shape.name() = "shape"
fun Circle.name() = "circle"

val s: Shape = Circle()
println(s.name())   // "shape" — chosen by the declared type, not the runtime type

p: Extensions can be declared on nullable types (`fun String?.orDash() = this ?: "—"`), which lets you call them safely on null values. Extension properties cannot have backing fields; they are computed every time.

mistakes.bad: Nesting `let` inside `apply` inside `run`
mistakes.good: Keep scope functions one level deep, or use named local variables.

mistakes.bad: Expecting extension functions to be overridden
mistakes.good: Use a member function or interface for polymorphism.

mistakes.bad: Using `also` to transform a value
mistakes.good: `also` returns the original object; use `let` or `map` to transform.

qa.q: When would you choose an extension function over a utility class?
qa.a: When the function reads naturally as an operation on the type, for example `dp.toPx()` or `view.show()`. It improves discoverability through autocomplete and keeps call sites readable. Keep extensions in a focused file or scope them (e.g. private or in a specific module) so they do not pollute common types like String across the whole codebase.

lessons.title: Higher-order functions, inline and generics
body: A lambda passed to a normal function is compiled to an object. `inline` copies the function body and the lambda into the call site, avoiding that allocation and allowing non-local `return`. Use `noinline` and `crossinline` when a lambda is stored or called from another context.
`reified` type parameters (only in inline functions) keep the type at runtime. Variance: `out T` means a producer (`List<out T>`), `in T` means a consumer (`Comparator<in T>`).
lessons.tip: Remember PECS from Java: Producer Extends, Consumer Super. In Kotlin that is out and in.

code.title: reified and variance in practice
code.src:
inline fun <reified T> Gson.fromJson(json: String): T =
    fromJson(json, object : TypeToken<T>() {}.type)

interface Source<out T> { fun next(): T }          // only produces T
interface Sink<in T> { fun put(item: T) }          // only consumes T

fun copy(from: Source<Number>, to: Sink<Int>) { /* ... */ }

val users: List<User> = gson.fromJson(json)        // no Class token needed

p: Without `inline`, each lambda becomes an object implementing `Function1`, and capturing lambdas allocate a new object at every call. An `inline` function's body and its lambda arguments are copied into the call site, so there is no allocation and no virtual call.

This is why standard functions like `map`, `filter` and `let` are inline. It also allows **non-local returns**: `return` inside an inlined lambda returns from the outer function. Large inline functions increase bytecode size, so only inline small functions that take lambdas.

`noinline` marks a lambda parameter that should stay an object, for example because you store it in a field. `crossinline` keeps the lambda inlined but forbids non-local returns, which is needed when the lambda is called from another context such as a `Runnable`.

JVM generics are erased at runtime: a `List<String>` is just a `List`. `reified` works around this inside inline functions by substituting the real type at each call site, so `T::class` and `is T` work.

Variance answers "can a `List<Dog>` be used where a `List<Animal>` is expected?" For a read-only `List<out T>`, yes (covariant). For a `MutableList<T>`, no (invariant), because you could add a Cat to a list of Dogs.

code.title: Why MutableList is invariant

mistakes.bad: Marking big functions `inline` "for performance"
mistakes.good: Inline only small higher-order functions; otherwise you bloat bytecode.

mistakes.bad: Checking `if (x is List<String>)`
mistakes.good: Generic types are erased; check `is List<*>` and the element types separately.

mistakes.bad: Making a producer interface invariant
mistakes.good: Use `out T` when a type only returns T, so callers get flexible subtyping.

qa.q: Explain `inline fun <reified T> Activity.start()` and why reified needs inline.
qa.a: Normally a generic `T` is erased, so the function cannot know which class to start. Because the function is inline, its body is copied into each call site, where the compiler knows the actual type, and `reified` lets it use `T::class.java` there. Without inline, there is no call-site copy, so the type information would not exist at runtime.

lessons.title: Introduction
body: In Compose you describe UI as a function of state: `UI = f(state)`. When state changes, Compose re-runs (**recomposes**) only the functions that read that state, and skips the rest when their inputs are unchanged.
Interview questions centre on three ideas: where state lives (hoisting), what triggers recomposition, and how to run side effects safely from a function that can run many times.
points: Composables are idempotent and side-effect free
Recomposition can be frequent, out of order, and skipped
State hoisting: state down, events up
lessons.tip: A stateless composable plus a thin stateful wrapper is the pattern interviewers want to see. It is easy to preview and test.

code.title: A stateless, hoisted composable

deep.h: How Compose turns functions into UI
p: The Compose compiler plugin rewrites every `@Composable` function so it receives a hidden `Composer` parameter. As your functions run, they record what they emit into a data structure called the **slot table**. That tree of nodes becomes your UI.

When state that a composable read changes, Compose marks that composable's **restart scope** as invalid and, on the next frame, re-runs just that function. That is recomposition. Functions whose inputs did not change can be skipped.

deep.h: The three phases of a frame
p: Every frame goes through **composition** (what to show, runs your composable functions), **layout** (measure and place) and **drawing** (render pixels). State read during composition triggers recomposition; state read only during layout or drawing (for example inside `Modifier.offset { }` or `drawBehind { }`) skips composition and is cheaper.

deep.h: Why composables must be side-effect free
p: Compose may run a composable many times, skip it, run it on a different thread in future, or throw away the result. If a composable writes to a database or logs an analytics event directly, that side effect happens an unpredictable number of times. Side effects belong in effect handlers or event callbacks.

code.title: Side effect in composition (wrong) vs callback (right)

mistakes.bad: Calling a ViewModel function directly in the composable body
mistakes.good: Call it from an event callback or a `LaunchedEffect`.

mistakes.bad: Passing the whole ViewModel into deep child composables
mistakes.good: Pass only the state and lambdas each child needs.

mistakes.bad: Applying `padding` before `clickable` and wondering why the touch area is small
mistakes.good: Modifier order matters; each modifier wraps the next.

qa.q: What is recomposition and what triggers it?
qa.a: Recomposition is Compose re-running composable functions to update the UI. It is triggered when a `State` object that a composable read during composition changes. Compose tracks those reads automatically through the snapshot system. Only the affected restart scopes re-run, and composables whose parameters are stable and unchanged are skipped.

lessons.title: State, remember and hoisting
body: `mutableStateOf` creates observable state; `remember` keeps it across recompositions; `rememberSaveable` also keeps it across rotation and process death. Without `remember`, state resets on every recomposition.
Hoist state to the lowest common parent that needs it. Screen-level state belongs in a ViewModel exposed as `StateFlow`, collected with `collectAsStateWithLifecycle`.
points: derivedStateOf to limit recomposition from fast-changing state
Immutable state objects; avoid mutable collections in state
lessons.tip: Always pass key = { it.id } to lazy lists. It keeps item state stable when the list reorders, and interviewers notice when it is missing.

code.title: derivedStateOf for a scroll-dependent button

p: `mutableStateOf` creates a value inside Compose's **snapshot system**. When a composable reads `state.value` during composition, Compose records that read. When something writes a new value, the snapshot is applied and every composable that read it is scheduled to recompose.

This is also why mutating a regular `ArrayList` inside state does nothing: the state object's reference did not change, so no write was recorded. Use `mutableStateListOf` or replace the list with a new one.

`remember` stores a value in the slot table at the composable's **position** in the tree. On recomposition, the same call at the same position returns the stored value. If the composable leaves the composition (for example an `if` turns false), the value is forgotten.

`remember(key) { }` recalculates when the key changes. `rememberSaveable` additionally writes the value into the saved instance state Bundle, so it survives rotation and process death; it needs a type that fits in a Bundle or a custom `Saver`.

Hoist state to the **lowest common ancestor** that reads it, and no higher. UI element state (a text field's focus, an expanded card) can live in the composable. Screen state that comes from data or must survive navigation belongs in the ViewModel.

code.title: Mutating vs replacing a list

mistakes.bad: `val count = mutableStateOf(0)` without `remember`
mistakes.good: State is recreated every recomposition; wrap it in `remember`.

mistakes.bad: Storing state in a mutable `ArrayList` inside `mutableStateOf`
mistakes.good: Replace the list, or use `mutableStateListOf`.

mistakes.bad: Keeping screen data in `remember` instead of the ViewModel
mistakes.good: It is lost on navigation and process death; move it to the ViewModel.

qa.q: What is the difference between `remember` and `rememberSaveable`?
qa.a: `remember` keeps a value across recompositions while the composable stays in composition, but it is lost on configuration change and process death. `rememberSaveable` also saves the value into the instance state Bundle, so it survives rotation and process death. Use rememberSaveable for small UI state the user would expect to keep, such as text being typed or a selected tab.

lessons.title: Recomposition and stability
body: Compose can **skip** a composable when all its parameters are stable and equal to last time. Primitive types, `String`, function types and classes annotated `@Immutable` or `@Stable` are stable; a `List` interface or a class with `var`s may not be.

Lambdas that capture unstable values, reading state too high in the tree, and creating new objects during composition all cause extra recompositions. Strong skipping mode (default in newer Compose compilers) relaxes some of these rules.
points: Read state as late as possible (lambda modifiers like offset { })
lessons.tip: Explain the three phases, composition → layout → drawing, and say a state read in a later phase skips the earlier ones.

code.title: Deferring a state read to the layout phase

p: When a parent recomposes, Compose compares each child's new parameters with the previous ones. If every parameter is **stable** and `equals` the old value, the child is skipped. A type is stable if Compose can trust that a change will be reported: immutable values, primitives, `String`, function types, and classes marked `@Stable` or `@Immutable`.

Collections from `kotlin.collections` (`List`, `Map`) are interfaces that could be mutable, so they were unstable before **strong skipping mode**. With strong skipping (default since Kotlin 2.0.20), unstable parameters are compared by instance identity instead, so many more composables can skip.

A lambda that captures values is a new object when those values change. Compose automatically remembers lambdas whose captures are stable. Method references to a ViewModel (`vm::onClick`) are stable as long as the ViewModel instance is the same.

Use **Layout Inspector** in Android Studio to see recomposition and skip counts per composable. Enable **Compose compiler reports** to see which classes are inferred as unstable and which functions are not skippable.

code.title: Enabling compiler reports

mistakes.bad: Adding `@Stable` to a class with mutable `var` fields that are not State
mistakes.good: You are lying to the compiler; the UI can miss updates.

mistakes.bad: Reading a fast-changing state (scroll, animation) high in the tree
mistakes.good: Read it in the lowest composable, or in a layout or draw lambda.

mistakes.bad: Optimising stability before measuring
mistakes.good: Check recomposition counts first; most screens do not need tuning.

qa.q: A list item recomposes every time the user types in a search box above the list. Why, and how do you fix it?
qa.a: The search text state is probably read in a composable that also contains the list, so the whole scope recomposes on each keystroke, and the item parameters may be unstable. Fix it by reading the text only inside the search field composable, passing stable item models (immutable data classes) to items, using `key`s in LazyColumn, and checking with Layout Inspector that items are now skipped.

lessons.title: Side effects
body: Composable functions must not perform side effects directly, because they can run any number of times. Use effect handlers. `LaunchedEffect(key)` runs a coroutine when it enters composition and restarts when the key changes. `DisposableEffect` adds cleanup. `SideEffect` publishes to non-Compose code after each successful recomposition.
`rememberCoroutineScope` gives a scope for event handlers like a button click. `rememberUpdatedState` lets a long-running effect see the latest value without restarting.
lessons.tip: LaunchedEffect(Unit) means "once per entering composition", not "once ever". It runs again after the composable leaves and comes back.

code.title: One-time events and lifecycle cleanup

p: `LaunchedEffect(key1, key2)` starts a coroutine when it enters composition, scoped to that position in the tree. If any key changes, the running coroutine is **cancelled** and a new one starts. When the composable leaves composition, the coroutine is cancelled. Choose keys carefully: they define when the effect restarts.
`DisposableEffect` works the same way but for non-coroutine resources: it runs setup on entry and `onDispose` on exit or when keys change.

A long-running effect captures the values present when it started. If a callback parameter changes later, the effect still calls the old one. `rememberUpdatedState(value)` gives the effect a State that always holds the latest value, without restarting the effect.

deep.h: Turning Compose state into a Flow
p: `snapshotFlow { state.value }` creates a Flow that emits whenever the state read inside it changes. It is the bridge for sending UI state, such as scroll position, to analytics or a ViewModel.

code.title: Report when the user scrolls past the first item

mistakes.bad: `LaunchedEffect(true)` to load data on every screen entry
mistakes.good: Load in the ViewModel `init` or on a trigger, so it does not reload on every return.

mistakes.bad: Using a changing value as a key when you do not want restarts
mistakes.good: Use stable keys and `rememberUpdatedState` for the changing value.

mistakes.bad: Launching coroutines with `GlobalScope` from a click handler
mistakes.good: Use `rememberCoroutineScope()` so work is cancelled when the UI leaves.

qa.q: What is the difference between LaunchedEffect and rememberCoroutineScope?
qa.a: LaunchedEffect starts a coroutine automatically as part of composition, and restarts it when its keys change; use it for work that should happen because the UI is showing something. rememberCoroutineScope returns a scope you launch from yourself in event handlers such as onClick, for example to animate a scroll. Both cancel their work when the composable leaves composition.

lessons.title: Lists, navigation and performance
body: `LazyColumn` composes only visible items. Give items stable `key`s and a `contentType` so slots can be reused. Avoid heavy work inside item lambdas; precompute in the ViewModel.

For release performance, use **Baseline Profiles** (Compose is a library, so the first run is interpreted without them), keep R8 enabled, and always measure in a release build. Debug builds are much slower and give misleading results.
points: key and contentType in lazy lists
Precompute display strings in the ViewModel
lessons.tip: "I measured in a release build with a Baseline Profile" is the sentence that separates real Compose performance work from guesswork.

code.title: An efficient lazy list

p: `LazyColumn` composes and lays out only the items that fit on screen, plus a small buffer. As you scroll, items leaving the screen are disposed and new ones are composed. Since Compose 1.5+, the slots of off-screen items are **reused** for new items of the same `contentType`, which reduces work further.
Keys tell Compose which item is which. Without them, item state is tied to position, so inserting at the top shifts all state down by one and animations look wrong.

deep.h: Why release builds and Baseline Profiles matter
p: Compose ships as a library, not as part of the OS, so its code is not pre-compiled on the device. On first launches ART interprets or JIT-compiles it, which causes jank. A **Baseline Profile** lists hot code paths, and the Play Store (or ProfileInstaller) uses it to compile them ahead of time on install.
Debug builds also disable optimisations and add debugging checks, so they can be several times slower. Performance numbers from debug builds are not meaningful.

Pass IDs between destinations, not whole objects; the destination loads the object from the repository. That keeps navigation arguments small and makes process death safe, because only the ID needs to be restored.

code.title: Type-safe navigation with an ID

mistakes.bad: Using `items(list)` without a `key` for lists that change
mistakes.good: Pass `key = { it.id }` so state and animations follow the item.

mistakes.bad: Formatting dates and prices inside item composables
mistakes.good: Prepare display strings in the ViewModel.

mistakes.bad: Passing large objects as navigation arguments
mistakes.good: Pass an ID; load data in the destination ViewModel.

qa.q: How do you make a Compose screen scroll smoothly on low-end devices?
qa.a: Measure first in a release build with a Macrobenchmark or JankStats. Then: add a Baseline Profile; use keys and contentType in lazy lists; keep item composables light by precomputing data; load images with a library like Coil at the right size; defer fast-changing state reads to layout or draw; and confirm with Layout Inspector that items are being skipped.

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Coroutines are a **lightweight** way to write asynchronous code that reads like sequential code. A `suspend` function can pause without blocking its thread, so thousands of coroutines can share a few threads.
On Android you launch coroutines in a scope tied to a lifecycle, usually `viewModelScope` or `lifecycleScope`, so work is cancelled automatically when the screen goes away.
lessons.tip: Coroutines work great with lifecycle-aware components like ViewModel and lifecycleScope: cancellation comes for free.

code.title: Launching a coroutine

p: Android has one main thread that draws the screen. If you call the network on it, the app freezes. The old fixes were threads and callbacks. Threads are expensive (each one needs about 1 MB of memory), and callbacks nest inside each other until the code is hard to read. People call that "callback hell".

A coroutine lets you write the same work as plain top-to-bottom code. When it has to wait, for example for a network response, it **suspends**: it steps aside and frees the thread so other work can run. When the answer arrives, it continues from the same line.

code.title: Callbacks vs a coroutine

p: A coroutine is just an object that remembers where it stopped. You can start 100,000 coroutines easily, while 100,000 threads would crash the app. Many coroutines share a small pool of threads, taking turns whenever one of them suspends.

The Kotlin compiler turns each `suspend` function into a small **state machine**. Each place where it can pause becomes a numbered step. When the function suspends, it saves its local variables and the step number in an object called a `Continuation`, then returns. When the result is ready, the continuation is called and the function jumps back to the saved step.
That is why suspend functions have no special threads or magic. It is ordinary code, rewritten by the compiler so it can stop and resume.

mistakes.bad: Thinking `suspend` moves work to a background thread
mistakes.good: It does not. Use `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)` for blocking work.

mistakes.bad: Calling `Thread.sleep()` inside a coroutine
mistakes.good: Use `delay()`, which suspends instead of blocking the thread.

mistakes.bad: Starting coroutines with `GlobalScope`
mistakes.good: Use a scope tied to a lifecycle, like `viewModelScope`.

qa.q: What is the difference between a thread and a coroutine?
qa.a: A thread is managed by the operating system and is expensive to create and switch. A coroutine is a lightweight task managed by Kotlin that runs on top of threads. Many coroutines can share one thread, because a coroutine gives up the thread whenever it suspends. Coroutines also come with structured concurrency, so cancelling a scope cancels all its work.

lessons.title: Coroutine basics
body: `launch` starts a coroutine that returns a `Job` and is used for fire-and-forget work. `async` returns a `Deferred<T>`, and you call `await()` for the result; use it to run independent work in parallel.

A `suspend` function can only be called from another suspend function or a coroutine. Suspending is cooperative: the function gives up its thread at suspension points such as `delay`, `withContext` or a network call written with suspend.
points: suspend means "can pause", not "runs in background"
runBlocking only in tests or main functions
lessons.tip: A suspend function does not switch threads by itself. Saying "suspend makes it run in the background" is a red flag in interviews.

code.title: Parallel calls with async

p: `launch` starts a coroutine and returns a `Job`. Use it when you do not need a result back, such as saving to the database or sending analytics. You can use the Job to cancel the work or wait for it with `join()`.

deep.h: async: start and get a result later
p: `async` starts a coroutine and returns a `Deferred<T>`, which is a promise of a value. Call `await()` to get it. The real power is running independent tasks **at the same time**: start several `async` blocks, then await them all.

code.title: Sequential vs parallel

p: Mark a function `suspend` when it calls other suspend functions or needs to wait. You can only call it from a coroutine or from another suspend function. That rule keeps waiting code from accidentally running on the main thread without a coroutine around it.
`runBlocking` starts a coroutine and **blocks** the current thread until it finishes. It is useful in `main()` functions and old-style tests, but never on the Android main thread.

mistakes.bad: Using `async` and never calling `await()`
mistakes.good: Use `launch` if you do not need the result; errors in async are only seen at await.

mistakes.bad: Writing `async { }.await()` right away
mistakes.good: That is just sequential code; call the function directly.

mistakes.bad: Using `runBlocking` in app code
mistakes.good: It freezes the thread; use a scope and `launch`.

qa.q: When would you use async instead of launch?
qa.a: Use async when you need a result back and especially when you want to run several independent calls in parallel, then combine the results with await. Use launch for work that does not return anything, such as saving data. Both should be started inside a proper scope so they are cancelled together.

lessons.title: Coroutine scopes and dispatchers
body: A **scope** owns the coroutines started in it; cancelling the scope cancels all of them. A **dispatcher** decides which thread runs the code: `Main` for UI, `IO` for blocking I/O (a large, elastic pool), `Default` for CPU work (as many threads as cores).

Good practice is **main-safety**: every suspend function in your data layer switches to the right dispatcher itself with `withContext`, so callers can call it from Main. Inject dispatchers so tests can replace them.
lessons.tip: GlobalScope work is not tied to any lifecycle and leaks easily. If something must outlive a screen, use an application-level scope you control, or WorkManager.

code.title: Main-safe repository with an injected dispatcher

p: A scope is a container for coroutines. Every coroutine is started inside one, and when the scope is cancelled, all its coroutines are cancelled too. On Android you rarely make your own: `viewModelScope` is cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared, and `lifecycleScope` when the Activity or Fragment is destroyed.

**Dispatchers.Main**: the UI thread. Use it to update views. **Dispatchers.IO**: a big pool for waiting work like files, databases and network. **Dispatchers.Default**: a pool sized to the number of CPU cores, for heavy calculations like sorting large lists or parsing JSON.
`Dispatchers.Main.immediate` runs right away if you are already on the main thread, instead of posting to the queue. `viewModelScope` uses it by default.

code.title: Switching threads with withContext

p: Every coroutine carries a `CoroutineContext`, a small set of settings: the `Job`, the dispatcher, an optional name and an optional exception handler. You combine them with `+`, like `Dispatchers.IO + CoroutineName("sync")`. Children inherit their parent's context unless you override parts of it.

mistakes.bad: Updating the UI from `Dispatchers.IO`
mistakes.good: Switch back to Main, or return the value and let the caller update the UI.

mistakes.bad: Using IO for heavy CPU work
mistakes.good: Use `Dispatchers.Default`; IO is for waiting, not computing.

mistakes.bad: Hard-coding dispatchers inside classes
mistakes.good: Pass them in through the constructor so tests can replace them.

qa.q: What does "main-safe" mean?
qa.a: A main-safe function can be called from the main thread without freezing it. The function itself switches to the right dispatcher with withContext for any blocking or heavy work. Repositories and data sources should be main-safe, so ViewModels can call them from viewModelScope without thinking about threads.

lessons.title: Structured concurrency and cancellation
body: Coroutines form a tree: a parent waits for its children, and cancelling a parent cancels its children. That is **structured concurrency**, and it prevents leaked work.

Cancellation is **cooperative**. Suspending functions from kotlinx check for it automatically, but a tight CPU loop must call `ensureActive()` or `yield()`. Never swallow `CancellationException` in a catch-all, or cancelled work keeps running.
lessons.tip: runCatching { } also catches CancellationException. Mention this subtle trap if the interviewer asks about error handling.

code.title: Cancellation-safe work

p: Coroutines form a family tree. When you `launch` inside another coroutine, the new one is a **child**. A parent always waits for its children to finish, and cancelling a parent cancels every child. This makes it hard to leak work: when the screen closes, the whole tree stops.
`coroutineScope { }` creates a child scope inside a suspend function. It finishes only when all coroutines inside it finish, and if one fails, the others are cancelled.

Cancelling a coroutine does not stop it instantly. It marks the Job as cancelled, and the next time the code reaches a **suspension point** (like `delay`, `withContext` or a Room query), it throws `CancellationException`, which ends the coroutine cleanly.
If your code is a long loop with no suspension points, it never notices. Add `ensureActive()` or check `isActive` inside the loop.

code.title: A loop that respects cancellation

p: Use `try { } finally { }` to close resources when a coroutine is cancelled. If the cleanup itself needs to suspend, wrap it in `withContext(NonCancellable)`. To give up after a time limit, use `withTimeout(ms)` (throws) or `withTimeoutOrNull(ms)` (returns null).

mistakes.bad: Catching `Exception` and ignoring it inside a coroutine
mistakes.good: This also catches CancellationException; rethrow it or catch narrower types.

mistakes.bad: Long CPU loops with no `ensureActive()`
mistakes.good: Add a check so cancellation can stop the work.

mistakes.bad: Using `launch` from a different scope inside a function
mistakes.good: Use `coroutineScope { }` so child work belongs to the caller.

qa.q: What happens to child coroutines when the parent is cancelled?
qa.a: They are all cancelled too. Each child gets a CancellationException at its next suspension point and finishes. The parent completes only after all children are done. This is structured concurrency: work started in a scope cannot outlive the scope.

lessons.title: Error handling
body: An uncaught exception in a child of a regular `Job` cancels the parent and all siblings. With a `SupervisorJob` (or `supervisorScope`), a failing child does not affect its siblings. `viewModelScope` uses a SupervisorJob.

`launch` propagates exceptions to its parent immediately; `async` holds them until `await()`. A `CoroutineExceptionHandler` is a last resort for logging and only works on root coroutines, not to recover.
points: try/catch around the suspend call itself
lessons.tip: Classic question: "a SupervisorJob is the parent of two children and one throws. What happens?" Only that child fails; the sibling and parent continue.

code.title: Independent children with supervisorScope

deep.h: How failures travel up the tree
p: With a normal `Job`, if a child throws, the error goes up to the parent. The parent then cancels all its other children and fails too. This is good when the tasks belong together, such as loading three parts of one screen: if one fails, the rest are useless.

A `SupervisorJob` (or `supervisorScope { }`) changes the rule: a failing child does not cancel its siblings or its parent. Use it when tasks are independent, like syncing contacts and photos. `viewModelScope` uses a SupervisorJob, so one failed request does not kill the whole ViewModel.

code.title: Handling errors in the ViewModel

deep.h: launch vs async errors, and the handler
p: In `launch`, an exception is thrown as soon as it happens. In `async`, it is stored and thrown when you call `await()`. A `CoroutineExceptionHandler` is only a last place to log crashes; it works only on top-level coroutines and cannot recover from errors. Prefer `try/catch` close to the call.

mistakes.bad: Putting `try/catch` around `launch { }` instead of inside it
mistakes.good: The launch returns immediately; catch inside the coroutine.

mistakes.bad: Expecting CoroutineExceptionHandler to recover
mistakes.good: It only logs; handle errors with try/catch.

mistakes.bad: Using one `Job()` as parent for independent tasks
mistakes.good: Use `SupervisorJob()` so one failure does not stop the rest.

qa.q: In a supervisorScope, one child throws. What happens to the other children and the scope?
qa.a: The other children keep running and the scope does not fail. Only the failing child is cancelled. Its exception still needs handling, either with try/catch inside that child or a CoroutineExceptionHandler, otherwise it is reported as uncaught.

lessons.title: Testing coroutines
body: Use `runTest` from kotlinx-coroutines-test. It skips `delay`s with virtual time so tests run instantly. Replace `Dispatchers.Main` with a test dispatcher via `Dispatchers.setMain` in a JUnit rule.
Pass a `StandardTestDispatcher` or `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` into classes that take a dispatcher, and use `advanceUntilIdle()` to run pending work.
lessons.tip: Injecting dispatchers is what makes this test possible. Tie testability back to the design decision.

code.title: A ViewModel test

deep.h: Why testing coroutines needs special tools
p: Real coroutines use real threads and real time. A test that waits for `delay(5000)` would take 5 seconds, and code on `Dispatchers.Main` crashes in unit tests because there is no Android main thread. The `kotlinx-coroutines-test` library fixes both.

`runTest { }` runs your test in a coroutine with a **virtual clock**. When the code calls `delay(5000)`, the clock jumps ahead instantly. `advanceTimeBy(ms)` moves time forward by a set amount, and `advanceUntilIdle()` runs everything that is waiting.

code.title: A Main dispatcher rule

p: `StandardTestDispatcher` queues new coroutines and runs them only when you advance time or call `advanceUntilIdle()`. That gives you full control over order. `UnconfinedTestDispatcher` runs new coroutines right away, which is simpler for most ViewModel tests.

mistakes.bad: Using real `Thread.sleep` in tests
mistakes.good: Use `runTest` and virtual time.

mistakes.bad: Forgetting to set the Main dispatcher
mistakes.good: Use a JUnit rule with `Dispatchers.setMain`.

mistakes.bad: Creating a new TestDispatcher inside the class under test
mistakes.good: Inject the same dispatcher the test controls.

qa.q: How do you test a ViewModel that calls a repository on Dispatchers.IO?
qa.a: Inject the dispatcher into the repository or ViewModel instead of hard-coding Dispatchers.IO. In the test, pass a TestDispatcher, set it as Main with a rule, run the test inside runTest, and call advanceUntilIdle before asserting. Use a fake repository so the test is fast and predictable.

articles.title: Best practices for coroutines in Android

lessons.title: Introduction
body: A `Flow` is an asynchronous stream of values. Most flows are **cold**: nothing runs until someone collects, and each collector gets its own run.
`StateFlow` and `SharedFlow` are **hot**: they exist independently of collectors. StateFlow always has a current value (great for UI state); SharedFlow broadcasts events to any number of subscribers.
lessons.tip: Explain cold vs hot with a cassette tape (each listener starts from the beginning) and a radio station (you hear whatever is on now).

code.title: A cold flow

p: A suspend function returns **one** value later. A `Flow` returns **many** values over time, like a stream of search results, location updates or rows from a database that keep changing. You read a flow with `collect`, which runs your code for each value.
Flows are built on coroutines, so they support cancellation and suspend functions inside them.

deep.h: Cold flows: nothing happens until you collect
p: The code inside `flow { }` does not run when you create the flow. It runs only when someone calls `collect`, and it runs again from the start for each new collector. That is why a flow from Retrofit or Room is safe to create anywhere: it does no work until it is collected.

code.title: Creating and collecting

p: `flow { emit(x) }` for custom logic. `flowOf(1, 2, 3)` for fixed values. `list.asFlow()` to turn a collection into a flow. `callbackFlow { }` to wrap a listener-based API. Room and DataStore return flows for you.

mistakes.bad: Expecting a flow to start when it is created
mistakes.good: It starts on `collect`; nothing runs before that.

mistakes.bad: Collecting the same cold network flow in two places
mistakes.good: Each collector repeats the request; share it with `stateIn` or `shareIn`.

mistakes.bad: Calling `collect` on the main thread outside a coroutine
mistakes.good: `collect` is a suspend function; call it inside a coroutine.

qa.q: What is the difference between a cold flow and a hot flow?
qa.a: A cold flow starts its work only when collected and runs separately for every collector, like playing a recording from the start. A hot flow, such as StateFlow or SharedFlow, is active on its own and every collector sees the values currently being sent, like tuning in to a live radio station.

lessons.title: Operators
body: Intermediate operators (`map`, `filter`, `onEach`, `debounce`, `distinctUntilChanged`) build a new flow and run nothing. Terminal operators (`collect`, `first`, `toList`, `launchIn`) start it.

The `flatMap` family differs in concurrency: `flatMapLatest` cancels the previous inner flow when a new value arrives (perfect for search), `flatMapConcat` runs them one after another, and `flatMapMerge` runs them concurrently. `combine` emits when either input changes; `zip` pairs values one-to-one.
lessons.tip: This one snippet answers half the Flow interview: debounce, flatMapLatest, error handling and stateIn.

code.title: Search-as-you-type

p: Intermediate operators like `map`, `filter` and `onEach` take a flow and return a new flow. They do not run anything yet. You chain them into a pipeline, and the whole pipeline runs when a terminal operator such as `collect` or `first()` is called.

code.title: A small pipeline

p: `combine(a, b)` emits a new value whenever **either** flow emits, using the latest from both. It is perfect for UI state built from several sources, such as user settings plus data. `zip(a, b)` pairs values one by one and waits for both, so it is used less often.

Sometimes each value starts a new flow, like each search query starting a new search. `flatMapLatest` cancels the previous search when a new query arrives, so you only get results for the latest text. `flatMapConcat` waits for each inner flow to finish, and `flatMapMerge` runs them all at once.

code.title: combine for screen state

mistakes.bad: Using `flatMapMerge` for search
mistakes.good: Old results can arrive after new ones; use `flatMapLatest`.

mistakes.bad: Doing heavy work in `map` on the main thread
mistakes.good: Add `.flowOn(Dispatchers.Default)` after the heavy operators.

mistakes.bad: Using `zip` to combine UI sources
mistakes.good: Use `combine`; zip waits for both and pairs values one-to-one.

qa.q: What is the difference between combine and zip?
qa.a: combine emits whenever any input emits, always using the latest value from each input. zip waits until each input has a new value and pairs them in order, first with first, second with second. For UI state from several sources, combine is almost always the right choice.

lessons.title: StateFlow and SharedFlow
body: `StateFlow` holds one value, needs an initial value, replays the latest value to new collectors, and **conflates**: equal consecutive values are dropped and slow collectors see only the latest. Use it for UI state.

`SharedFlow` is configurable (`replay`, `extraBufferCapacity`, `onBufferOverflow`) and has no current value. For one-off UI events, a `Channel` received as a flow guarantees each event is handled once, even while no one is collecting.
lessons.tip: WhileSubscribed(5000) keeps the upstream alive for 5 seconds, so a rotation does not restart the work. Explain why that number is used.

code.title: State plus one-off events in a ViewModel

deep.h: StateFlow: a value that can change
p: `StateFlow` always holds one current value, which you read with `.value`. New collectors immediately get the current value, then every change after that. If you set the same value again, nothing is sent. This makes it a great fit for screen state.

code.title: Exposing state from a ViewModel

p: `SharedFlow` sends values to all current collectors and has no single current value. You choose how many old values new collectors get with `replay`. It suits things many parts of the app listen to, such as "user logged out" or "cart changed" events.

A cold flow from a repository can be turned into a hot one with `stateIn` or `shareIn`, so several collectors share one upstream instead of repeating the work. `SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5000)` keeps it running while someone is collecting, plus five seconds. That covers screen rotation without restarting the work, but stops it when the user really leaves.

code.title: Turning a repository flow into state
code.src:
val articles: StateFlow<List<Article>> = repo.articles()
    .stateIn(
        scope = viewModelScope,
        started = SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000),
        initialValue = emptyList()
    )

mistakes.bad: Exposing `MutableStateFlow` publicly
mistakes.good: Expose a read-only `StateFlow` so only the ViewModel changes it.

mistakes.bad: Using StateFlow for one-time events like "show toast"
mistakes.good: StateFlow keeps the last value; use a Channel or event in state.

mistakes.bad: `_state.value = _state.value.copy(...)` from many coroutines
mistakes.good: Use `_state.update { }`, which is safe against lost updates.

qa.q: Why use WhileSubscribed(5000) in stateIn?
qa.a: It keeps the upstream flow active only while the UI is collecting, plus a 5-second grace period. During rotation the UI stops collecting for a moment; the grace period means the data is not reloaded. When the user leaves the screen for longer, the upstream stops and saves battery and network.

lessons.title: Collecting safely on Android
body: Collecting in `lifecycleScope.launch { }` alone keeps collecting while the app is in the background, wasting resources and possibly crashing on UI updates. Use `repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)` in Views, or `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` in Compose.

`flowOn` changes the dispatcher of the **upstream** only; the collector keeps its own context. Never use `withContext` inside `flow { }` to emit from a different context; that breaks context preservation and throws.
lessons.tip: Forgetting awaitClose in callbackFlow leaks the listener. It is a favourite follow-up question.

code.title: Wrapping a callback API

p: If you collect a flow in `lifecycleScope.launch { }`, it keeps collecting while the app is in the background, because lifecycleScope is only cancelled when the Activity is destroyed. The flow keeps doing work nobody can see, and updating views while stopped can even crash.

`repeatOnLifecycle(Lifecycle.State.STARTED)` starts collecting when the screen becomes visible and cancels when it is hidden, then starts again next time. In Compose, `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` does the same thing for you and gives you a `State` to read.

code.title: Views and Compose

p: `flowOn(Dispatchers.IO)` moves the work **above** it to another dispatcher, while your `collect` stays where it was. To turn a listener API into a flow, use `callbackFlow { }`: register the listener, send values with `trySend`, and unregister in `awaitClose { }`, which runs when collecting stops.

mistakes.bad: Collecting in `lifecycleScope.launch` without repeatOnLifecycle
mistakes.good: Wrap the collect in `repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED)`.

mistakes.bad: Using `collectAsState()` for Android UI
mistakes.good: Prefer `collectAsStateWithLifecycle()` so collection stops in the background.

mistakes.bad: Forgetting `awaitClose` in callbackFlow
mistakes.good: Always unregister the listener in `awaitClose`.

qa.q: What does flowOn change?
qa.a: flowOn changes the dispatcher used by the operators and the flow builder above it, the upstream. It does not change where collect runs. So you can do heavy mapping on Dispatchers.Default with flowOn and still collect and update the UI on the main thread.

lessons.title: Backpressure, errors and testing
body: Flows are sequential by default: the producer suspends until the collector finishes each value. `buffer()` runs producer and collector concurrently, `conflate()` drops intermediate values, and `collectLatest` cancels slow handling when a new value arrives.
`catch` handles upstream errors only; exceptions thrown in `collect` are not caught by it. Test flows with **Turbine**: `flow.test { assertEquals(x, awaitItem()) }`.
lessons.tip: Because StateFlow conflates, a fast Loading → Data change may skip Loading in tests. Know this before an interviewer asks why your test is flaky.

code.title: Testing a flow with Turbine

deep.h: When the producer is faster than the collector
p: By default a flow is sequential: after `emit`, the producer waits until the collector has finished with that value. If collecting is slow, the producer slows down too. That is safe, but sometimes you want them to run independently.

`buffer()` lets the producer keep emitting into a queue while the collector works. `conflate()` drops values the collector did not get to and keeps only the newest, which is great for things like progress or sensor data. `collectLatest { }` cancels the work for the old value as soon as a new one arrives.

code.title: Only render the latest progress

p: `catch { }` handles errors from operators **above** it and can emit a fallback value. It does not catch errors thrown inside your `collect` block. `retry(3)` or `retryWhen { }` restarts the flow after an error, and you can add a delay to back off between tries.

code.title: Retry with backoff, then fallback

mistakes.bad: Expecting `catch` to handle errors thrown in `collect`
mistakes.good: Move risky work into `onEach` before `catch`, then call `collect()`.

mistakes.bad: Retrying forever on any error
mistakes.good: Retry only network errors, a few times, with a delay.

mistakes.bad: Using `buffer` when you only need the latest value
mistakes.good: Use `conflate` or `collectLatest`.

qa.q: What is the difference between conflate and collectLatest?
qa.a: conflate drops values the collector was too busy to receive, but finishes processing the current value. collectLatest cancels the processing of the current value as soon as a newer one arrives and starts again with the new value. Use collectLatest when processing an old value is pointless, like rendering a search result that is already out of date.

articles.title: Use Kotlin coroutines with lifecycle-aware components

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Good architecture keeps code easy to change and test. Android's recommended app architecture has a **UI layer** (screens and ViewModels), a **data layer** (repositories and data sources) and an optional **domain layer** (use cases).
Two rules make it work: **separation of concerns** (each class has one job) and **unidirectional data flow** (state flows down, events flow up).
points: UI layer, domain layer, data layer
lessons.tip: Start any architecture answer with the data flow, then the layers. Name the trade-off: more layers mean more files for small apps.

code.title: The layers in one flow

p: Without structure, screens talk directly to the network, the database and each other. Then one change breaks three places, and nothing can be tested without a phone. Architecture is about **who is allowed to know about whom**, so each part can change and be tested on its own.

**UI layer**: what the user sees (Activities, Fragments, composables) plus ViewModels that hold screen state. **Data layer**: repositories that decide where data comes from, and data sources that talk to the network, database or files. **Domain layer** (optional): use cases that hold business rules shared by several screens.
Arrows point one way: UI uses domain or data, domain uses data, and data knows nothing about the UI. That one-way rule is what keeps the app easy to change.

State flows **down** from the ViewModel to the UI. Events flow **up** from the UI to the ViewModel. The UI never changes state directly; it asks the ViewModel, which updates state, which the UI then shows. This makes it easy to see why the screen looks the way it does.

code.title: UDF in one screen

mistakes.bad: Calling Retrofit directly from an Activity
mistakes.good: Go through a ViewModel and a repository.

mistakes.bad: Letting the data layer import UI classes
mistakes.good: Keep arrows one way; the data layer returns plain models.

mistakes.bad: Adding every layer to a tiny app
mistakes.good: Start simple; add a domain layer only when logic is shared or complex.

qa.q: What is a single source of truth?
qa.a: It means each piece of data has exactly one owner that is allowed to change it, and everyone else reads from that owner. For screen state, the ViewModel is the owner. For app data, usually the local database is the owner and the network only updates it. This avoids two copies of the same data disagreeing.

lessons.title: MVVM and the ViewModel
body: The ViewModel holds and exposes UI state, survives configuration changes and outlives the View. It must **never** hold a reference to a View, Activity or Fragment context, or it will leak them.
Expose one immutable state object (`StateFlow<ScreenUi>`) instead of many separate LiveData fields. That avoids inconsistent combinations, such as loading and error showing at the same time.
points: No Context or View references (use AndroidViewModel only if needed)
lessons.tip: If asked "MVVM vs MVP", say MVVM's ViewModel does not know the View, so it survives rotation and is easier to test.

code.title: A single UI state

p: A ViewModel prepares and keeps the data a screen needs. It survives rotation, so data is not reloaded every time the phone turns. It also gives you `viewModelScope`, which cancels work when the screen is gone for good.
It must not know about views. No `TextView`, no `Activity`, no `Fragment` references. If it held one, the old Activity could never be freed after rotation.

Each Activity or Fragment has a `ViewModelStore`. When the Activity is recreated for a configuration change, Android keeps the store and hands it to the new Activity, so `by viewModels()` returns the same object. When the Activity finishes for real, the store calls `onCleared()` on each ViewModel and `viewModelScope` is cancelled.

code.title: One state, small functions

p: In MVP, the Presenter holds a reference to the View and calls methods on it like `view.showLoading()`. That breaks on rotation and needs careful attach and detach. In MVVM, the ViewModel just exposes state and the View observes it, so the ViewModel never needs to know if a View exists.

mistakes.bad: Passing an Activity context into the ViewModel
mistakes.good: Use `@ApplicationContext` via DI, or move that work elsewhere.

mistakes.bad: Exposing many separate LiveData fields
mistakes.good: Expose one state object so the UI never sees a half-updated mix.

mistakes.bad: Loading data in the Fragment and storing it in the ViewModel
mistakes.good: Let the ViewModel load data itself, usually in `init`.

qa.q: Why should a ViewModel not hold a reference to a View or Activity?
qa.a: The ViewModel lives longer than the Activity: it survives rotation while the Activity is destroyed and recreated. If it kept a reference, the old Activity and its whole view tree could not be garbage collected, which is a memory leak, and calls on it could crash. The ViewModel should only expose state that the current View observes.

lessons.title: MVI and unidirectional data flow
body: MVI models every user action as an **intent** (event), processes it with a reducer `(state, event) -> state`, and renders one immutable state. The flow is strictly one way, which makes behaviour predictable and easy to replay and debug.
The cost is boilerplate and the need to handle one-off effects (navigation, toasts) separately from state.
points: Pure reducers are easy to unit test
lessons.tip: Interviewers like a balanced view: MVI shines on complex screens with many interacting inputs, MVVM is enough for simple ones.

code.title: A minimal reducer

p: MVI stands for Model, View, Intent. The user does something (an **intent**, also called an action or event). A **reducer** takes the current state and the event and returns a new state. The **view** draws that state. Everything goes round in one circle.

code.title: A complete MVI loop

p: The reducer is a plain function with no Android code, so it is easy to test: give it a state and an event and check the result. Because every change goes through one place, you can log every event and replay bugs exactly.

Not everything is state. Navigation, showing a snackbar or opening a browser happen once. Keep those as **effects**, sent through a `Channel`, or model them in state and clear them after the UI handles them.

mistakes.bad: Calling the network inside the reducer
mistakes.good: Keep the reducer pure; do I/O in the ViewModel and send the result as an event.

mistakes.bad: Putting navigation in state without clearing it
