mistakes.good: Use an effect channel, or clear the flag after navigating.

mistakes.bad: Using MVI for a simple static screen
mistakes.good: MVVM with one state object is enough there.

qa.q: What is the main benefit of a pure reducer in MVI?
qa.a: A pure reducer always gives the same new state for the same old state and event, with no side effects. That makes state changes predictable, easy to unit test without Android, and easy to debug, because you can log and replay the sequence of events that led to any bug.

lessons.title: Repository, single source of truth and offline-first
body: A repository hides where data comes from. The usual pattern is that the **database is the single source of truth**: the UI observes Room, and the network only refreshes the database. That gives offline support and consistency for free.
Map network models (DTOs) and database entities to domain models at the boundary, so API changes do not ripple through the app.
points: Repository as the only entry point to data
Database as single source of truth
lessons.tip: Say "the UI never reads the network directly" when describing offline-first. It is the core idea in one line.

code.title: Offline-first repository

p: A repository is the one place the rest of the app asks for data. It hides the details: whether data came from memory, the database or the network, how it is cached, and how errors are mapped. ViewModels do not care. That also makes it easy to swap the real repository for a fake in tests.

deep.h: Offline-first: the database is the truth
p: In an offline-first app, the UI only ever reads from the local database, usually as a Flow. To refresh, the repository fetches from the network and **writes to the database**. The database emits the new rows, and the UI updates on its own. If there is no internet, the user still sees the saved data.

code.title: Read from DB, refresh from network

p: **DTOs** match the JSON from the server. **Entities** match database tables. **Domain models** are what the app actually uses. Small mapping functions convert between them. This seems like extra work, but when the API renames a field, you change one mapper instead of every screen.

mistakes.bad: Showing network data directly and also saving it
mistakes.good: Show only what comes from the database to avoid two truths.

mistakes.bad: Passing DTOs all the way to the UI
mistakes.good: Map to domain or UI models at the repository boundary.

mistakes.bad: Throwing raw `HttpException` to the ViewModel
mistakes.good: Map errors to simple app errors in the repository.

qa.q: Why should the UI observe the database instead of the network response?
qa.a: Because the database then becomes the single source of truth. The UI always shows one consistent copy of the data, it works offline, and any update, whether from a refresh, a background sync or a user edit, automatically reaches every screen that observes it. The network's only job is to keep the database fresh.

lessons.title: Clean Architecture and modularisation
body: Clean Architecture puts business rules in the centre (domain), with no Android dependencies, and frameworks at the edges. Dependencies point inward, and outer layers implement interfaces the inner layers define.

Splitting a large app into Gradle modules (`:core:data`, `:feature:checkout`) speeds up builds, enforces boundaries and lets teams work independently. Feature modules should depend on core modules, not on each other.
points: Use cases for reusable business logic
lessons.tip: Do not claim Clean Architecture is always right. Mention you would add a domain layer only when logic is shared or complex.

code.title: A typical module graph

p: The idea: keep your business rules (what the app does) separate from details (which database, which network library, which UI toolkit). Business rules sit in the middle and do not import Android classes. Details depend on the middle, never the other way round.
In practice on Android: the domain module has use cases and plain Kotlin models; the data module implements repository interfaces the domain declares; the UI calls use cases or repositories.

A use case is a small class that does one thing, like `PlaceOrderUseCase`. It is worth adding when the logic is used in more than one screen, or when it combines several repositories. Naming it with `operator fun invoke` lets you call it like a function.

code.title: A focused use case

p: Splitting the app into Gradle modules (for example `:core:network`, `:core:database`, `:feature:cart`) makes builds faster, because only changed modules recompile. It also enforces rules: if `:feature:cart` does not depend on `:feature:profile`, it simply cannot call its code. Features talk through shared core modules and navigation routes.

mistakes.bad: Use cases that only call one repository function
mistakes.good: Call the repository directly until real logic appears.

mistakes.bad: Feature modules depending on each other
mistakes.good: Share code through core modules; navigate with routes.

mistakes.bad: Putting Android classes in the domain layer
mistakes.good: Keep domain pure Kotlin so it is easy to test and reuse.

qa.q: When would you add a domain layer to an Android app?
qa.a: When business logic is shared by several ViewModels, when it combines several repositories, or when it is complex enough that it deserves its own tests. For a small app or simple screens, the domain layer just adds files without benefit, so I would start without it and add use cases when duplication or complexity appears.

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Dependency injection means a class receives its dependencies instead of creating them. That makes classes testable (pass a fake) and swappable (another implementation), and it centralises object lifetimes.
On Android the standard tool is **Hilt**, built on **Dagger**. Dagger generates the wiring code at compile time, so errors show up during the build instead of as crashes at runtime.
points: Compile-time graph (Dagger/Hilt) vs runtime service locator (Koin)
lessons.tip: Contrast Hilt (compile-time, safer, slower builds) with Koin (runtime, simpler, errors at runtime). A balanced answer scores better than a favourite.

code.title: Constructor injection

p: Imagine a `CheckoutViewModel` that creates its own `RazorpayGateway()` inside. You cannot test checkout without hitting a real payment service, and you cannot switch to another provider without editing the ViewModel. With dependency injection, the ViewModel just asks for a `PaymentGateway` in its constructor. Someone else decides which one to give it.
That "someone else" can be you, writing the wiring by hand, or a library like Hilt that writes it for you.

code.title: Manual DI first

p: Manual wiring is fine for a few classes. In a real app, hundreds of objects depend on each other, some must be single instances, and some must live only as long as a screen. A DI library builds this **dependency graph** for you and manages how long each object lives.

Dagger and Hilt check the whole graph while building the app and generate plain Java code to create objects. A missing binding is a build error, and there is no reflection at runtime. Koin resolves objects at runtime: setup is simpler and builds are faster, but a missing binding is a crash you find only when that code runs.

mistakes.bad: Creating dependencies inside classes with `SomeService()`
mistakes.good: Ask for them in the constructor.

mistakes.bad: Using DI as a global lookup (`get()` everywhere)
mistakes.good: Inject through constructors so dependencies are visible.

mistakes.bad: Mocking everything in tests
mistakes.good: Prefer simple fakes that implement the interface.

qa.q: What problems does dependency injection solve?
qa.a: It removes hard-coded creation of dependencies, so classes can be tested with fakes and implementations can be swapped. It centralises how objects are built and how long they live, such as one OkHttpClient for the whole app. It also makes each class's dependencies visible in its constructor, which makes the code easier to understand.

lessons.title: Hilt setup and components
body: Annotate the `Application` with `@HiltAndroidApp`, Android classes with `@AndroidEntryPoint`, and ViewModels with `@HiltViewModel`. Hilt provides a fixed hierarchy of **components**, each tied to an Android lifetime.

`SingletonComponent` lives as long as the app, `ActivityRetainedComponent` survives rotation, `ViewModelComponent` matches a ViewModel, and `ActivityComponent` and `FragmentComponent` match their owners. A child component can use bindings from its parents, not the other way round.
lessons.tip: Know that SavedStateHandle and @ApplicationContext are available without writing a module. Interviewers like that detail.

code.title: Wiring a ViewModel

deep.h: The three annotations you need first
p: `@HiltAndroidApp` on your `Application` class starts Hilt and creates the app-level container. `@AndroidEntryPoint` on an Activity, Fragment, View or Service lets Hilt inject fields into it. `@HiltViewModel` with an `@Inject constructor` lets Hilt create ViewModels, which you get with `by viewModels()` or `hiltViewModel()`.

deep.h: Components are containers with a lifetime
p: Hilt creates a container (component) for each Android lifetime. `SingletonComponent` lives as long as the app. `ActivityRetainedComponent` survives rotation. `ViewModelComponent` lives as long as one ViewModel. `ActivityComponent`, `FragmentComponent` and `ViewComponent` match those objects.
Components are nested: an Activity-level object can use anything from the app level, but an app-level object cannot use something from an Activity, because the Activity may not exist.

code.title: Field injection in an Activity

deep.h: What Hilt gives you for free
p: Without writing any module, you can inject `@ApplicationContext context: Context`, `@ActivityContext`, `SavedStateHandle` into ViewModels, and the Activity or Fragment itself in their components.

mistakes.bad: Using an injected field before `super.onCreate()`
mistakes.good: Injection happens in `super.onCreate()`; use fields after it.

mistakes.bad: Forgetting `@AndroidEntryPoint` on the host Activity of an annotated Fragment
mistakes.good: Every parent must be an entry point too.

mistakes.bad: Injecting an Activity-scoped object into a singleton
mistakes.good: Singletons cannot depend on shorter-lived objects.

qa.q: What is the difference between SingletonComponent and ActivityRetainedComponent?
qa.a: SingletonComponent lives for the whole app process. ActivityRetainedComponent lives as long as an Activity logically exists, so it survives configuration changes but is destroyed when the Activity finishes. Use the retained one for things that should be shared by one screen flow but not kept forever.

lessons.title: Modules: @Provides and @Binds
body: Use a module when you cannot use constructor injection: interfaces, third-party classes (Retrofit, OkHttp, Room) or objects that need configuration.

`@Binds` maps an interface to its implementation and generates less code; it must be abstract. `@Provides` runs your code to build an instance. Put both kinds in separate modules, or put `@Provides` in a companion object.
lessons.tip: Why is @Binds better than @Provides for interfaces? It generates no factory method body, so builds are faster and the generated code smaller.

code.title: Network module

p: Hilt can create any class that has an `@Inject constructor`. Modules are for the cases where it cannot: interfaces (which implementation should it use?), classes from libraries you do not own (Retrofit, Room, OkHttp) and objects built with builders.

`@Binds` says "when someone asks for this interface, give them this implementation". It is an abstract function with no body, so Hilt generates very little code. `@Provides` is a normal function that builds and returns an object; use it when you need code to create the object.

code.title: Both kinds of modules

p: When a class asks for `NotesRepository`, Hilt looks for a binding in the current component and its parents. Here it finds `@Binds`, which points to `NotesRepositoryImpl`, which has an `@Inject constructor` needing `NotesDao`, which comes from `@Provides`. All of this is checked at build time.

mistakes.bad: Using `@Provides` to return `NotesRepositoryImpl(dao)` by hand
mistakes.good: Add `@Inject` to the constructor and use `@Binds`.

mistakes.bad: Installing a module in the wrong component
mistakes.good: Install in the component whose lifetime matches the objects.

mistakes.bad: Building Retrofit in many places
mistakes.good: Provide one instance in a singleton module.

qa.q: Why prefer @Binds over @Provides for interfaces?
qa.a: @Binds only tells Dagger which implementation to use, so it generates less code and no extra factory method, which keeps builds faster and the app smaller. @Provides needs a function body that Dagger has to call. Use @Provides only when you must write code to construct the object.

lessons.title: Scopes and qualifiers
body: Without a scope annotation, Hilt creates a **new instance every time** one is requested. A scope (`@Singleton`, `@ActivityRetainedScoped`, `@ViewModelScoped`) makes one instance per component. Scope only what must be shared or is expensive, because scoped objects stay in memory for the component's lifetime.
**Qualifiers** distinguish two bindings of the same type, for example two OkHttpClients or two dispatchers.
points: Scope annotation must match the component
lessons.tip: Over-scoping to @Singleton is a common mistake. Mention it as a memory concern when asked about scopes.

code.title: Qualifying dispatchers

p: By default Hilt creates a **new object every time** someone asks for it. A scope annotation says "create one and reuse it for the life of this component". `@Singleton` = one per app. `@ActivityRetainedScoped` = one per Activity across rotation. `@ViewModelScoped` = one per ViewModel.

Scope objects that are expensive to create (OkHttpClient, the database) or that hold shared state (an in-memory cache, a session manager). Do not scope everything: a scoped object stays in memory for the whole component lifetime, even if no one uses it anymore.

deep.h: Qualifiers: two of the same type
p: If you need two `OkHttpClient`s (one with auth, one without) or two dispatchers, Hilt cannot tell which you want. A qualifier is a small annotation that gives each binding a name, checked by the compiler.

code.title: Two clients, two qualifiers

mistakes.bad: Marking every class `@Singleton`
mistakes.good: Scope only shared or expensive objects.

mistakes.bad: Using `@Named("x")` strings everywhere
mistakes.good: Custom qualifiers are type-safe and refactor-friendly.

mistakes.bad: Putting a `@ViewModelScoped` binding in SingletonComponent
mistakes.good: The scope must match the component it is installed in.

qa.q: What happens if you do not add a scope to a binding?
qa.a: Hilt creates a new instance every time the dependency is requested. That is the right default for small, stateless objects. If an object holds shared state or is expensive, add a scope that matches how long it should live, such as @Singleton for an app-wide OkHttpClient.

lessons.title: Testing and assisted injection
body: In instrumented tests, annotate the test with `@HiltAndroidTest`, use `HiltAndroidRule`, and replace production modules with `@TestInstallIn`. For plain unit tests you usually do not need Hilt at all: call the constructor with fakes.
When an object needs both injected dependencies and a runtime value (an ID), use **assisted injection** with `@AssistedInject` and an `@AssistedFactory`.
points: Unit tests: just call the constructor
lessons.tip: Saying "my unit tests do not need Hilt because I use constructor injection" shows you understand why DI exists.

code.title: Assisted injection

p: If your classes use constructor injection, most unit tests do not need Hilt at all. Create the class with `FakeRepository()` and call its functions. Tests stay fast and simple.

For instrumented tests that run the real app, annotate the test with `@HiltAndroidTest`, add `HiltAndroidRule`, and swap production modules with `@TestInstallIn(components = [...], replaces = [ProdModule::class])`. Every test then gets your fake instead of the real thing.

code.title: Swapping a module in tests

p: Some objects need both injected dependencies and a value known only at runtime, such as a download ID. Mark the runtime parameter with `@Assisted`, the constructor with `@AssistedInject`, and create a factory interface with `@AssistedFactory`. You inject the factory and call `create(id)`.

mistakes.bad: Adding Hilt to plain unit tests
mistakes.good: Construct the class directly with fakes.

mistakes.bad: Using `@UninstallModules` in every test class
mistakes.good: Prefer one `@TestInstallIn` module shared by all tests.

mistakes.bad: Passing runtime IDs through a singleton setter
mistakes.good: Use assisted injection or SavedStateHandle.

qa.q: How would you give a ViewModel both an injected repository and a screen argument like an item ID?
qa.a: For navigation arguments, the simplest way is SavedStateHandle: Hilt injects it into the ViewModel and it contains the arguments, so you read the ID from it. For other runtime values, use assisted injection with an @AssistedFactory, and in Compose, hiltViewModel can take a creation callback for assisted ViewModels.

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Most Android apps talk to a REST or GraphQL backend using **Retrofit** on top of **OkHttp**. Retrofit turns an annotated interface into HTTP calls; OkHttp does the actual work: connection pooling, HTTP/2, gzip, caching and interceptors.
Interviews test the full path: making calls main-safe, handling errors and timeouts, authentication with token refresh, caching, and security.
points: Retrofit builds requests, OkHttp executes them
lessons.tip: Share one OkHttpClient across the app (use newBuilder() for variants). Each client has its own connection pool and thread pool.

code.title: A Retrofit API

p: When you call a Retrofit function, Retrofit reads its annotations (`@GET`, `@Query`, `@Body`), builds an HTTP request, and hands it to OkHttp. OkHttp runs it through your interceptors, finds or opens a connection, sends it, and passes the response back through the interceptors. Retrofit then uses a converter (Moshi, kotlinx.serialization) to turn the JSON into your Kotlin class.
With `suspend` functions, Retrofit runs the call off the main thread for you, so the function is main-safe.

Opening a secure connection is slow: a DNS lookup, a TCP handshake and a TLS handshake. OkHttp keeps a **connection pool** and reuses connections to the same server, and HTTP/2 can send many requests over one connection at once. That is why you should share a single `OkHttpClient` instead of creating one per request.

code.title: One client, one Retrofit
code.src:
val client = OkHttpClient.Builder()
    .connectTimeout(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .readTimeout(20, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
    .build()

val retrofit = Retrofit.Builder()
    .baseUrl("https://api.example.com/v1/")      // must end with /
    .client(client)
    .addConverterFactory(Json.asConverterFactory("application/json".toMediaType()))
    .build()

val api: ShopApi = retrofit.create()

p: If a suspend function returns `T`, Retrofit throws `HttpException` for non-2xx responses. If it returns `Response<T>`, you get the status code, headers and error body and decide yourself. Use `Response<T>` when you need headers or want to handle error codes without exceptions.

mistakes.bad: Creating a new OkHttpClient per request
mistakes.good: Share one client so connections and threads are reused.

mistakes.bad: A base URL without a trailing slash
mistakes.good: Retrofit requires the base URL to end with `/`.

mistakes.bad: Parsing large JSON on the main thread with a manual call
mistakes.good: Let Retrofit do it in a suspend function.

qa.q: What is the difference between Retrofit and OkHttp?
qa.a: OkHttp is the HTTP client that actually sends requests: connections, pooling, HTTP/2, caching, interceptors and TLS. Retrofit sits on top and turns an annotated Kotlin interface into OkHttp calls, including converting JSON to objects. Retrofit makes APIs easy to declare; OkHttp does the network work.

lessons.title: Interceptors
body: An interceptor sees every request and response. **Application interceptors** (`addInterceptor`) run once per call and see the final response. **Network interceptors** (`addNetworkInterceptor`) run for each network round-trip, including redirects, and see what goes on the wire.
Typical uses: adding auth and common headers, logging (debug builds only), request IDs, and rewriting cache headers.
lessons.tip: Never log Authorization headers or bodies in release builds. Mention redactHeader on the logging interceptor.

code.title: An auth header interceptor

p: Interceptors form a chain, like layers of an onion. Each one gets the request, can change it, calls `chain.proceed(request)` to pass it on, and then sees the response on the way back. That makes them perfect for anything that applies to every request: headers, logging, metrics, retries.

code.title: Timing every request

p: An **application interceptor** (`addInterceptor`) runs once per call. It does not see redirects or cached responses separately, so it is the right place for auth headers and logging. A **network interceptor** (`addNetworkInterceptor`) runs for every real network request, including redirects, and sees the exact bytes sent. It does not run when the answer comes from the cache.
`HttpLoggingInterceptor` is great while developing. Add it only in debug builds, and use `redactHeader("Authorization")` so tokens never appear in logs.

mistakes.bad: Calling `chain.proceed()` twice in one interceptor
mistakes.good: Call it once; use an Authenticator or retry logic for repeats.

mistakes.bad: Logging request bodies in release builds
mistakes.good: Add the logging interceptor only for debug, with redaction.

mistakes.bad: Doing slow work (disk reads) inside interceptors
mistakes.good: Keep interceptors fast; cache values like tokens in memory.

qa.q: Where would you add an auth header, and why there?
qa.a: In an application interceptor, because it runs once per call regardless of redirects or retries and applies to every request made by that client. For refreshing the token after a 401, I would use an OkHttp Authenticator instead, because it is designed to retry with new credentials.

lessons.title: Authentication and token refresh
body: When an access token expires, the server returns 401. OkHttp's **Authenticator** is called on a 401 and can return a new request with a refreshed token, or null to give up.
With many parallel requests, all of them can hit 401 at once. Synchronise the refresh so only one call refreshes and the others reuse the new token, and stop retrying after a limit to avoid loops.
points: Store tokens securely (EncryptedSharedPreferences or DataStore + Keystore)
lessons.tip: The "compare the token we sent with the current one" check is the detail that shows you have built this in production.

code.title: A single-flight token refresh

p: Most APIs give you a short-lived **access token** (say 15 minutes) for normal calls, and a long-lived **refresh token** used only to get new access tokens. When the access token expires, the server answers `401 Unauthorized`. The app should quietly refresh and retry, without the user noticing.

OkHttp calls your `Authenticator` automatically when a response is 401. You return a new request with a fresh token, and OkHttp retries it. Return `null` to give up, for example when the refresh token is also invalid; then log the user out.

If five requests fail with 401 at the same moment, you do not want five refresh calls. Use a lock so only one thread refreshes. The others wait, then notice the token already changed and simply retry with the new one.

code.title: A refresh with a mutex-style check

mistakes.bad: Refreshing tokens inside an interceptor for every request
mistakes.good: Refresh only on 401 using an Authenticator.

mistakes.bad: No limit on retries
mistakes.good: Stop after one retry, or the app loops forever on a bad refresh token.

mistakes.bad: Storing tokens in plain SharedPreferences
mistakes.good: Use encrypted storage backed by the Android Keystore.

qa.q: Five API calls fail with 401 at the same time. How do you make sure the token is refreshed only once?
qa.a: Put the refresh inside a lock in the Authenticator. The first thread refreshes and saves the new token. Each other thread, once it gets the lock, compares the token it used with the current saved token; if they differ, another thread already refreshed, so it just retries with the current token instead of refreshing again.

lessons.title: Errors, retries and caching
body: Model results explicitly: success, HTTP error (4xx/5xx with a body), network error (no connection, timeout) and unexpected errors. Retry only idempotent requests and transient failures, with exponential backoff and jitter.
OkHttp has an HTTP cache that honours `Cache-Control`. Give it a `Cache` directory and size, and let the server's headers decide freshness. For offline-first, cache in Room instead.
points: Typed results instead of throwing everywhere
Retry with backoff only for idempotent calls
lessons.tip: Mention exponential backoff with jitter: without jitter, all clients retry at the same moment and overload the server again.

code.title: A safe call wrapper

p: Not all errors are equal. **No connection or timeout** (`IOException`): maybe retry, show "check your connection". **4xx** (bad request, not found, forbidden): the request is wrong, retrying will not help. **5xx** (server error): maybe retry later. **Parsing errors**: a bug, report it. Treat each kind differently in the UI.

Only retry when it is safe and likely to help: network errors and some 5xx, and only for requests that can be repeated without harm (GET, or POST with an idempotency key). Wait longer each time (exponential backoff) and add a little randomness (jitter) so thousands of phones do not retry at the same instant.

code.title: Retry with exponential backoff

p: Give OkHttp a `Cache(dir, size)` and it will follow the server's `Cache-Control` headers. `max-age=60` means "use the saved copy for 60 seconds". With an `ETag`, OkHttp asks "has it changed?" and gets a tiny `304 Not Modified` if not, saving data. For true offline use, store data in Room instead.

mistakes.bad: Retrying a payment POST without an idempotency key
mistakes.good: Send a unique key so the server can ignore duplicates.

mistakes.bad: Showing "Something went wrong" for every error
mistakes.good: Show different messages for offline, server and input errors.

mistakes.bad: Retrying 400 or 401 errors
mistakes.good: Fix the request or refresh auth; do not blindly retry.

qa.q: Why add jitter to retry delays?
qa.a: If many devices fail at the same moment, for example during a server outage, plain exponential backoff makes them all retry at exactly the same times, creating traffic spikes that can knock the server over again. Adding a small random amount to each delay spreads the retries out.

lessons.title: Security
body: All traffic should use HTTPS; Android blocks cleartext by default from API 28. A **network security config** controls trusted certificates, debug overrides and cleartext exceptions.

**Certificate pinning** (OkHttp `CertificatePinner`) defends against compromised CAs but can lock users out if certificates rotate, so pin backup keys and plan the rotation. Never put secrets in the APK; anything shipped can be extracted.
points: HTTPS only; cleartext blocked by default
No API secrets in the app; use a backend
lessons.tip: Always say "with a backup pin" when you mention pinning. Pinning a single key is how apps break on certificate rotation day.

code.title: Certificate pinning
code.src:
val pinner = CertificatePinner.Builder()
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/AAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAA=")  // current key
    .add("api.example.com", "sha256/BBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBBB=")  // backup key
    .build()

val client = OkHttpClient.Builder().certificatePinner(pinner).build()

p: HTTPS encrypts traffic and proves you are talking to the real server. The server sends a certificate signed by a **certificate authority** (CA) that the phone already trusts. Since Android 9, plain HTTP is blocked by default, which is good. You can allow exceptions only in the network security config, ideally only for debug.

Pinning means the app also checks that the server's key matches one you expect. Even if someone tricks the phone into trusting a fake CA, the connection fails. The risk: if the server's certificate changes and the app does not know the new key, every request fails. Always pin a backup key and plan certificate updates.

deep.h: Secrets do not belong in the app
p: Anything inside the APK can be extracted with free tools, including `BuildConfig` strings and obfuscated code. Keys that must stay secret, such as a payment provider's secret key, stay on your server. The app calls your server, which calls the provider.

code.title: Debug-only trust for a local proxy
code.src:
<!-- res/xml/network_security_config.xml -->
<network-security-config>
    <base-config cleartextTrafficPermitted="false" />
    <debug-overrides>
        <trust-anchors>
            <certificates src="user" />     <!-- lets Charles/Proxyman work in debug only -->
        </trust-anchors>
    </debug-overrides>
</network-security-config>

mistakes.bad: Pinning only one certificate
mistakes.good: Pin the current and a backup key.

mistakes.bad: Shipping API secrets in BuildConfig
mistakes.good: Keep secrets on the server; the app only gets short-lived tokens.

mistakes.bad: Allowing cleartext traffic for the whole app
mistakes.good: Use HTTPS everywhere; allow exceptions only per domain if unavoidable.

qa.q: What is certificate pinning and what is its main risk?
qa.a: Pinning makes the app accept a server only if its certificate's public key matches a key built into the app, which blocks man-in-the-middle attacks even with a compromised certificate authority. The main risk is lockout: if the server changes its key and the app has no matching pin, all requests fail until users update. Pinning a backup key avoids that.

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Android gives you several places to keep data: **Room** (SQLite) for structured, queryable data; **DataStore** for small key-value settings; files in app-specific storage for blobs; and MediaStore or the Storage Access Framework for shared files.
Picking the right one, keeping disk work off the main thread, and migrating schemas safely are the core interview themes.
points: All disk I/O off the main thread
lessons.tip: If asked "SharedPreferences vs DataStore", say: DataStore is async, uses Flow, handles errors and is safe from main-thread disk I/O.

code.title: Choosing storage

deep.h: Where your app can save things
p: **App-specific storage** (`filesDir`, `cacheDir`) is private to your app, needs no permission and is deleted on uninstall. The system may clear `cacheDir` when space is low. **Shared storage** (photos, downloads) is visible to other apps and goes through MediaStore or the Storage Access Framework.

deep.h: Pick by the shape of the data
p: Small settings like dark mode or "has seen onboarding": **DataStore**. Lists of structured items you search, sort or relate (notes, messages, orders): **Room**. Big blobs like images or PDFs: **files**, with the file path stored in Room if needed. Secrets like tokens: encrypted storage backed by the Android **Keystore**.

code.title: Files in app-specific storage

p: Reading or writing disk can take tens of milliseconds, or much more on a slow phone. Room refuses to run queries on the main thread by default. For files, wrap the work in `withContext(Dispatchers.IO)`. Turn on `StrictMode` in debug builds to catch accidental disk access on the main thread.

mistakes.bad: Storing a big JSON list in SharedPreferences
mistakes.good: Use Room for lists; Preferences are loaded fully into memory.

mistakes.bad: Saving images inside the database as blobs
mistakes.good: Store files on disk and keep the path in the database.

mistakes.bad: Keeping auth tokens in plain text
mistakes.good: Encrypt them with a Keystore-backed key.

qa.q: How would you choose between Room, DataStore and files?
qa.a: I look at the data. Small key-value settings go in DataStore. Structured records that I need to query, sort, filter or observe go in Room. Large binary content like images or downloads goes in files in app-specific storage, with metadata in Room if I need to search it.

lessons.title: Room fundamentals
body: Room has three parts: `@Entity` (table), `@Dao` (queries) and `@Database` (holder). SQL queries are checked at **compile time**, which catches typos and missing columns before the app runs.
DAO methods can be `suspend` for one-shot work or return `Flow` to observe the table: Room re-emits whenever the tables used by the query change.
points: suspend for one-shot, Flow for observation
lessons.tip: Add indices for columns you filter or sort on. "How would you speed up this query?" usually wants an index.

code.title: Entity, DAO and an observable query

deep.h: How Room fits on top of SQLite
p: SQLite is the database built into Android. Using it directly means writing SQL strings, cursor loops and lots of boilerplate. Room is a layer on top: you describe tables as Kotlin classes, write queries in annotations, and Room generates the code at build time and checks your SQL against the tables.

An `@Entity` is a table; each property is a column. A `@Dao` is an interface with query methods. The `@Database` class lists entities, the version number, and gives you DAOs. Create one database instance for the whole app (usually through DI), because opening it is expensive.

code.title: Relations with @Relation

p: When a DAO method returns `Flow`, Room watches the tables used in the query. Any insert, update or delete on those tables makes the query run again and emit fresh results. That is how the UI updates by itself when data changes.

mistakes.bad: Creating a new database instance in each Activity
mistakes.good: Use one instance for the app, provided by DI.

mistakes.bad: Missing indices on foreign keys and filter columns
mistakes.good: Add `indices` for faster queries.

mistakes.bad: Using `allowMainThreadQueries()`
mistakes.good: Use suspend functions and Flow instead.

qa.q: How does a Room Flow know when to emit new data?
qa.a: Room tracks which tables each query reads. It registers an observer on those tables through its InvalidationTracker. When any write changes one of those tables, the tracker marks the query invalid, Room runs it again and the Flow emits the new result. Writes to unrelated tables do not trigger it.

lessons.title: Migrations
body: Every schema change needs a database version bump and a migration. Without one, Room throws at startup, or wipes data if you used `fallbackToDestructiveMigration()`, which is rarely acceptable for user data.
Prefer **auto-migrations** for simple changes (adding a column or table), write a manual `Migration` for complex ones, and export schemas so you can test every path with `MigrationTestHelper`.
points: Bump version on every schema change
AutoMigration with specs for renames and deletes
lessons.tip: Mention testing migrations from every old version that users may still have, not only the previous one.

code.title: Auto and manual migrations

p: Your users already have a database file on their phones with the old shape. When you add a column, the new app version expects the new shape. A migration is the set of steps that changes the old file into the new shape **without losing user data**.

For simple changes (new table, new column with a default), Room can write the migration for you. Turn on `exportSchema` so Room saves a JSON copy of each version's schema, then list `AutoMigration(from = 2, to = 3)`. For renames and deletions, add a small spec class so Room knows what you meant.

code.title: Auto migration with a rename

p: `MigrationTestHelper` creates a database at an old version, runs your migrations and checks the result against the exported schema. Test from **every** version your users might still have, not only the last one, because people skip updates.

mistakes.bad: Changing an entity without bumping the version
mistakes.good: Room crashes at startup; bump the version and add a migration.

mistakes.bad: Using `fallbackToDestructiveMigration()` for user data
mistakes.good: Only use it for caches you can rebuild.

mistakes.bad: Not committing exported schema files
mistakes.good: Commit them; migration tests and auto migrations need them.

qa.q: A user jumps from app version 1 straight to version 5. How does Room handle it?
qa.a: Room finds a path of migrations from 1 to 5, such as 1 to 2, 2 to 3, 3 to 4 and 4 to 5, and runs them in order. If any step is missing it throws, unless destructive fallback is enabled. You can also provide a direct 1-to-5 migration, which Room prefers because it is shorter.

lessons.title: DataStore
body: **Preferences DataStore** stores key-value pairs; **Proto DataStore** stores a typed object defined by a schema. Both expose data as a `Flow` and write transactionally with `edit` or `updateData`.
Create one DataStore instance per file (use the `preferencesDataStore` delegate at top level). Two instances for the same file throw an exception.
points: Reads are Flow, writes are suspend
Not for large or relational data
lessons.tip: SharedPreferences.apply() still blocks the main thread during onPause in some cases. That is a concrete reason to move to DataStore.

code.title: Preferences DataStore

p: SharedPreferences reads the whole file into memory and has a synchronous API, so reads on the main thread can freeze the app. `apply()` writes in the background but can still block the main thread while the app is pausing. Errors are silently ignored.
DataStore is built on coroutines and Flow. Reads are a Flow, writes are suspend functions run in a transaction, and errors are reported as exceptions you can handle.

**Preferences DataStore** stores simple keys and values, like SharedPreferences, with typed keys. **Proto DataStore** stores one typed object defined with a schema (Protocol Buffers), so you get type safety for a whole settings object.

code.title: Migrating from SharedPreferences

p: Sometimes you need the current value only once, for example at startup. Use `settings.data.first()` inside a coroutine. Avoid `runBlocking` on the main thread to read it; show a splash state while it loads instead.

mistakes.bad: Creating DataStore inside a function each time
mistakes.good: Declare it once at top level with the delegate.

mistakes.bad: Storing lists of records in DataStore
mistakes.good: Use Room for lists and relations.

mistakes.bad: Reading DataStore with `runBlocking` on Main
mistakes.good: Use `first()` in a coroutine and show a loading state.

qa.q: What problems does DataStore solve compared to SharedPreferences?
qa.a: It never blocks the main thread because reads are Flows and writes are suspend functions on a background dispatcher. Updates are transactional, so you do not get half-written values. Errors surface as exceptions instead of being silently ignored, and Proto DataStore adds type safety for whole objects.

lessons.title: Offline-first and sync
body: In an offline-first app, the UI reads only from the local database; writes go to the database first and are synced to the server later. Track pending changes (a `syncState` column or an outbox table) and push them with **WorkManager** when there is a network connection.
Plan for conflicts: last-write-wins with server timestamps is simple; field-level merging or versions are safer when users edit the same data on several devices.
points: Local database is the source of truth
Paging 3 with RemoteMediator for large lists
lessons.tip: Use unique work so repeated triggers do not stack up duplicate syncs.

code.title: Queueing a sync with WorkManager

p: The app works with whatever data it has, even with no internet. Reading always comes from the local database. Writes are saved locally first and the UI updates at once. A background job sends the changes to the server when possible.

Keep a table of pending changes (an **outbox**). Each row says what to send, like "mark note 42 as done". A WorkManager job reads the outbox, sends each change, and deletes the row on success. If the app is killed or the phone has no signal, the rows wait safely and are sent later.

code.title: Saving locally and queueing

p: Two devices can change the same item while offline. The simplest rule is **last write wins**: keep whichever change has the newer timestamp, using server time if possible. For important data, keep a version number and ask the user, or merge field by field.

mistakes.bad: Updating the UI only after the server confirms
mistakes.good: Update the local database first; sync in the background.

mistakes.bad: Using device time to resolve conflicts
mistakes.good: Prefer server timestamps or version numbers.

mistakes.bad: Starting a sync job for every single change
mistakes.good: Use unique work so many changes share one sync run.

qa.q: How would you build a notes app that works offline and syncs across devices?
qa.a: Room is the source of truth and the UI observes it. Edits are written to Room and an outbox table in one transaction. A unique WorkManager job with a network constraint pushes outbox items, then pulls server changes since the last sync token and writes them to Room. Conflicts are resolved with server-side version numbers, using last-write-wins for simple fields.

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Gradle turns source code and resources into an APK or App Bundle. The Android Gradle Plugin (AGP) adds Android tasks: resource merging, D8 dexing, R8 shrinking and signing.
Interviewers ask about build configuration (variants, flavours), dependency management, shrinking and obfuscation, and how to make builds faster in large projects.
lessons.tip: Explain compileSdk vs targetSdk vs minSdk in one line each. It is asked in almost every Android build question.

code.title: A minimal module build file

deep.h: What happens when you press Run
p: Gradle runs in three phases. **Initialization**: read `settings.gradle.kts` to find which modules exist. **Configuration**: run every module's `build.gradle.kts` to build a list (graph) of tasks. **Execution**: run only the tasks needed for what you asked, such as `assembleDebug`.

For an Android app, those tasks compile Kotlin to JVM bytecode, convert it to Android's DEX format with **D8**, merge and compile resources with **AAPT2**, shrink the code with **R8** in release builds, package everything into an APK or App Bundle, and sign it.

**compileSdk** is the Android version you compile against; it decides which APIs you can call. **minSdk** is the oldest Android version that can install your app. **targetSdk** tells the system which version's behaviour your app is ready for; newer behaviour changes switch on when you raise it. Google Play requires a recent targetSdk.

code.title: Calling a newer API safely

p: An APK is the installable file. An **Android App Bundle** (`.aab`) is what you upload to Play; Google builds smaller APKs from it for each device, containing only that device's screen density, CPU type and language. Users download less.

mistakes.bad: Doing slow work (network, reading files) in build scripts
mistakes.good: It runs on every sync during configuration; move it into tasks.

mistakes.bad: Raising targetSdk without reading the behaviour changes
mistakes.good: Check the release notes for that Android version and test.

mistakes.bad: Calling new APIs without a version check
mistakes.good: Guard with `Build.VERSION.SDK_INT` or use AndroidX compat helpers.

qa.q: What is the difference between compileSdk and targetSdk?
qa.a: compileSdk only affects compiling: which APIs your code can reference. targetSdk is put into the app and tells Android which version's behaviour changes your app has been tested with, so the system turns on newer rules such as permission changes. You usually keep both on the latest version.

lessons.title: Build types and product flavours
body: **Build types** describe how you build (`debug`, `release`, maybe `benchmark`); **product flavours** describe what you build (`free`/`paid`, `dev`/`prod`). Gradle combines them into **build variants** such as `prodRelease`.
Each variant can have its own source set (`src/prod/`), resources, `BuildConfig` fields and application ID suffix, so dev and prod builds can be installed side by side.
lessons.tip: Never put real secrets in buildConfigField. They end up as plain strings in the APK.

code.title: Environments as flavours

p: A build type describes **how** the app is built. `debug` is debuggable, unoptimised and signed with a debug key. `release` is minified with R8, optimised and signed with your real key. You can add more, like `benchmark` (release-like but profileable) or `staging`.

Flavours describe **what** you build: free and paid versions, or dev and prod environments. Flavours belong to **dimensions**; Gradle combines one flavour from each dimension with each build type. Two flavours times two build types gives four variants, like `devDebug` and `prodRelease`.

code.title: Different code per flavour

p: Each variant combines files from `src/main`, the flavour folder (`src/dev`), the build type folder (`src/debug`) and the combined folder (`src/devDebug`). For resources, the more specific folder wins. Classes cannot be overridden this way; put a class in each flavour folder, not in `main` too.

mistakes.bad: Using `if (BuildConfig.DEBUG)` branches all over the code
mistakes.good: Put environment differences in flavours or config objects.

mistakes.bad: Too many flavour dimensions
mistakes.good: Each dimension multiplies variants and build time; keep it small.

mistakes.bad: Same applicationId for dev and prod
mistakes.good: Use `applicationIdSuffix` so both can be installed together.

qa.q: What is the difference between a build type and a product flavour?
qa.a: A build type controls how the app is built, such as debuggable, minified and signing config, with debug and release by default. A product flavour controls what is built, such as a free or paid version or a dev or prod backend. Gradle combines them into build variants.

lessons.title: Dependencies and version catalogs
body: `implementation` hides a dependency from modules that depend on yours, so changes do not force them to recompile. `api` exposes it. Prefer `implementation` for faster incremental builds.
A **version catalog** (`gradle/libs.versions.toml`) keeps all versions in one place with type-safe accessors. **BOMs** (Compose, Firebase, OkHttp) align versions across a library family.
lessons.tip: Explaining why implementation speeds up builds (smaller recompilation surface) shows you understand Gradle, not just its syntax.

code.title: A version catalog
code.src:
# gradle/libs.versions.toml
[versions]
kotlin = "2.0.21"
compose-bom = "2024.10.01"

[libraries]
compose-bom = { group = "androidx.compose", name = "compose-bom", version.ref = "compose-bom" }
compose-ui = { group = "androidx.compose.ui", name = "ui" }

[plugins]
kotlin-android = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.android", version.ref = "kotlin" }

# build.gradle.kts
# implementation(platform(libs.compose.bom))
# implementation(libs.compose.ui)

p: When two libraries ask for different versions of the same library, Gradle picks the **highest** version by default. That is usually fine, but sometimes a newer version breaks the older user. `./gradlew :app:dependencies` shows the full tree and which version won.

With `implementation`, a dependency is private to your module: modules that depend on yours cannot see it. With `api`, it becomes part of your module's public surface. Use `api` only when your public classes expose types from that library. `implementation` means fewer modules recompile when the library changes.

A version catalog (`gradle/libs.versions.toml`) keeps every library and version in one file, and Gradle generates accessors like `libs.retrofit`. A **BOM** (bill of materials) is a published list of versions that work together, such as the Compose BOM. You import it once with `platform()` and then add its libraries without versions.

code.title: Using a BOM and a catalog
code.src:
dependencies {
    implementation(platform(libs.androidx.compose.bom))   // pins all Compose versions
    implementation(libs.androidx.compose.ui)              // no version needed
    implementation(libs.androidx.compose.material3)

    implementation(libs.retrofit)
    testImplementation(libs.junit)
    debugImplementation(libs.leakcanary)                  // only in debug builds
}

mistakes.bad: Using `api` everywhere "to be safe"
mistakes.good: Use `implementation` unless your public API exposes the library.

mistakes.bad: Hard-coding versions in each module
mistakes.good: Keep them in the version catalog.

mistakes.bad: Adding a whole big library for one small helper
mistakes.good: Check the app size impact; copy small helpers if allowed.

qa.q: Why does using implementation instead of api make builds faster?
qa.a: With implementation, the dependency is not part of the module's public interface, so modules that depend on yours do not see it. When that library changes, Gradle only recompiles your module, not every module above it. With api, the change leaks to all consumers and causes more recompilation.

lessons.title: R8: shrinking and obfuscation
body: In release builds, **R8** removes unused code (tree shaking), optimises and inlines it, and renames classes and members to short names. `isShrinkResources` also removes unused resources.

Code reached only by reflection (JSON models, some DI or serialization libraries) can be removed or renamed by mistake. Keep rules (`-keep`) tell R8 what to leave alone; many libraries ship their own consumer rules. Upload the `mapping.txt` file to deobfuscate crash stack traces.
points: Reflection is the usual cause of release-only crashes
lessons.tip: A crash that only happens in release is almost always R8 plus reflection. Say how you would find it: a minified debug build and the mapping file.

code.title: Release configuration

deep.h: What R8 does, step by step
p: **Shrinking**: starting from entry points (Activities, Services, anything in the manifest and keep rules), R8 follows every reference and removes code nothing reaches. **Optimising**: it inlines small functions, removes dead branches and merges classes. **Obfuscating**: it renames classes and members to short names like `a.b`, which also makes the app smaller.

R8 only sees normal code references. If a library finds your class by its name at runtime (reflection), for example Gson creating objects from JSON field names, R8 may have renamed or removed it. The release build then crashes or returns empty objects. A `-keep` rule tells R8 to leave those classes alone. Libraries like kotlinx.serialization and Moshi codegen avoid reflection and need fewer rules.

code.title: Keep rules and stack traces
code.src:
# proguard-rules.pro
-keep class io.droidly.data.remote.dto.** { *; }        # DTOs read by Gson via reflection
-keepattributes Signature, *Annotation*                  # generics and annotations at runtime

# Decode an obfuscated crash locally:
# retrace mapping.txt stacktrace.txt

p: R8 writes `mapping.txt`, a dictionary from short names back to real names. Upload it to Play Console and your crash reporter for every release, otherwise crash stack traces show `a.b.c()` and are almost useless.

mistakes.bad: Testing only debug builds before release
mistakes.good: Run a minified release build; many bugs appear only there.

mistakes.bad: Adding `-keep class ** { *; }` to fix a crash
mistakes.good: That disables shrinking; keep only what reflection needs.

mistakes.bad: Losing the mapping file for a release
mistakes.good: Archive it with each build and upload it automatically in CI.

qa.q: The app works in debug but crashes in release with a ClassNotFoundException. What do you check?
qa.a: It is almost certainly R8 removing or renaming a class used by reflection. I would reproduce with a minified build, decode the stack trace with the mapping file, find which library loads the class by name, and add a narrow keep rule or switch that library to code generation instead of reflection.

lessons.title: Faster builds
body: Large projects get slow builds from three things: configuration time, too much recompilation, and annotation processing. Fixes include the **configuration cache**, the **build cache**, modularisation with `implementation` dependencies, and **KSP** instead of kapt.
Measure before optimising: use a **build scan** or the Build Analyzer in Android Studio to see which tasks take the time.
points: Modularisation for parallel and incremental builds
lessons.tip: Quote a before and after ("clean build 6 min to 3 min") if you have one. Numbers make build answers credible.

code.title: gradle.properties for speed
code.src:
org.gradle.parallel=true
org.gradle.caching=true
org.gradle.configuration-cache=true
org.gradle.jvmargs=-Xmx4g -XX:+UseParallelGC
android.nonTransitiveRClass=true
kotlin.incremental=true

p: Slow builds usually come from: configuring many modules on every run, recompiling too much after a small change, annotation processors (especially kapt), and missing caches. Measure first: a **Build Scan** (`--scan`) or Android Studio's **Build Analyzer** shows which tasks and plugins take the most time.

The **build cache** reuses task outputs from earlier builds (or from teammates and CI, with a remote cache), so tasks whose inputs did not change are not run again. The **configuration cache** saves the result of the configuration phase, so Gradle can skip running every build script on the next build.

kapt runs Java annotation processors on Kotlin code by first generating Java stubs for all your Kotlin classes, which is slow. **KSP** reads Kotlin code directly and is often about twice as fast. Room, Hilt and Moshi all support KSP.

code.title: Switching Room to KSP

mistakes.bad: Optimising builds without measuring
mistakes.good: Use a build scan or Build Analyzer to find the slow tasks first.

mistakes.bad: One giant app module
mistakes.good: Split into modules so changes recompile less.

mistakes.bad: Keeping kapt when every processor supports KSP
mistakes.good: Move processors to KSP and remove the kapt plugin.

qa.q: How would you speed up a slow Android build in a large project?
qa.a: Measure with a build scan to find the biggest costs. Then enable the build and configuration caches, move annotation processing from kapt to KSP, use implementation instead of api, turn on non-transitive R classes, and modularise so a change touches fewer modules. In CI, add a remote build cache so developers reuse CI's outputs.
