lessons.title: Introduction
body: Performance questions are about what the user feels: how fast the app starts, whether scrolling is smooth, whether it runs out of memory, and how much battery it uses.
The winning approach is always the same: **measure, find the bottleneck, fix it, measure again**, in a release build on a real low-end device.
lessons.tip: Interviewers distrust "it felt faster". Always say what you measured, with what tool, on which device.

code.title: Measuring startup with Macrobenchmark

p: **Startup**: how long until the first useful screen. **Smoothness**: whether scrolling and animations stutter. **Stability**: crashes and "app not responding" (ANR) dialogs. **Resource use**: battery, data and storage. Google Play's **Android vitals** tracks crash rate, ANR rate and more, and poor numbers can hurt your Play Store visibility.
Debug builds are slow on purpose: no R8, extra checks, debugging enabled. Measure a release-like build. Use a real mid- or low-end phone, because your flagship hides problems your users see.

**Macrobenchmark**: repeatable numbers for startup and scrolling in CI. **Perfetto / system trace**: a timeline that shows what every thread did, frame by frame. **Android Studio profilers**: CPU, memory and network over time. **LeakCanary**: memory leaks in debug builds. **JankStats**: jank measured on real users' devices.

code.title: Marking your own sections in a trace

mistakes.bad: Measuring performance in debug builds
mistakes.good: Use a release or benchmark build type.

mistakes.bad: Testing only on a flagship phone
mistakes.good: Test on a low-end device too.

mistakes.bad: Optimising without a baseline number
mistakes.good: Record the current numbers first so you can prove improvement.

qa.q: How do you approach a "the app feels slow" complaint?
qa.a: First I make it specific: slow startup, janky scrolling, or a slow action. Then I reproduce it on a similar device with a release build, capture a system trace or Macrobenchmark, find the actual bottleneck in the trace, fix that one thing, and measure again to confirm the improvement. I add a benchmark in CI so it does not regress.

lessons.title: App startup
body: **Cold** start creates the process, the Application and the first Activity; **warm** start reuses the process; **hot** start only brings the Activity to the front. Time to initial display (TTID) and time to full display (TTFD, reported with `reportFullyDrawn`) are the key metrics.

Common wins: move work out of `Application.onCreate`, initialise SDKs lazily or in the background, avoid disk and network on the main thread, and ship **Baseline Profiles** so hot code paths are compiled ahead of time.
points: Lazy SDK initialisation and App Startup library
lessons.tip: Baseline Profiles can improve startup and early interactions substantially, especially for Compose apps. Mention them in any startup answer.

code.title: Lazy initialisation instead of Application.onCreate

p: **Cold start**: the app process does not exist. Android creates it, runs `Application.onCreate`, creates the Activity and draws the first frame. This is the slowest and most important case. **Warm start**: the process exists but the Activity must be recreated. **Hot start**: the Activity is just brought back to the front.

The usual suspects: SDKs initialised in `Application.onCreate` (analytics, ads, crash reporting all at once), content providers that libraries add to the manifest, reading disk or SharedPreferences on the main thread, a heavy first layout, and code that runs slowly because it has not been compiled yet.

Android compiles app code gradually as it runs. On first launches, much of your code is interpreted or JIT compiled, which is slower. A **Baseline Profile** is a list of the classes and methods used during startup and key journeys. Play ships it with the app, and Android compiles that code ahead of time at install, so the first launches are fast.

code.title: Generating a Baseline Profile

mistakes.bad: Initialising every SDK in `Application.onCreate`
mistakes.good: Initialise lazily or in the background unless the first frame needs it.

mistakes.bad: Reading SharedPreferences on the main thread at startup
mistakes.good: Load settings asynchronously and show a placeholder.

mistakes.bad: Forgetting `reportFullyDrawn()`
mistakes.good: Call it when real content shows, so TTFD is measured correctly.

qa.q: What is a Baseline Profile and why does it help startup?
qa.a: It is a list of the code paths your app uses during startup and important user journeys. It is packaged with the app, and on install Android compiles those paths ahead of time to machine code. Without it, that code would be interpreted or JIT compiled on the first runs, which is slower and causes jank.

lessons.title: Rendering and jank
body: At 60 Hz each frame has about 16 ms; at 120 Hz about 8 ms. A frame that misses its deadline is **jank**. Causes include heavy work on the main thread, deep or over-measured layouts, overdraw, large bitmaps and garbage-collection pauses.

Find it with **Perfetto** / system traces, the JankStats library, and the Profileable release build. In RecyclerView, use `DiffUtil` / `ListAdapter`, stable IDs and fixed sizes; in Compose, avoid unnecessary recompositions.
lessons.tip: notifyDataSetChanged() redraws everything and kills animations. Saying you replaced it with ListAdapter is a quick, concrete win.

code.title: ListAdapter with DiffUtil

p: To show 60 frames per second, each frame has about 16 milliseconds (8 ms at 120 Hz). On the main thread, Android handles input, runs animations, then measures, lays out and draws the views into a list of drawing commands. The **RenderThread** then sends them to the GPU. If the main thread is busy past the deadline, the frame is late and the user sees a stutter.

Doing work on the main thread while scrolling (decoding images, parsing JSON, database calls). Layouts that are measured many times (deep nested weights, `RelativeLayout` inside `RelativeLayout`). Creating many objects in `onDraw` or `onBindViewHolder`, which triggers garbage collection. Full list reloads with `notifyDataSetChanged()`.

code.title: Keep onBindViewHolder cheap

p: Record a system trace while scrolling and look at frames marked red or yellow. Click a long frame and you see exactly which functions ran on the main thread. Adding your own `trace("name") { }` sections makes this even easier to read.

mistakes.bad: Decoding full-size images for small thumbnails
mistakes.good: Request images at the view size with an image loader.

mistakes.bad: Formatting data in `onBindViewHolder`
mistakes.good: Prepare display strings in the ViewModel.

mistakes.bad: Using `notifyDataSetChanged()` for small updates
mistakes.good: Use `ListAdapter` with `DiffUtil`.

qa.q: What is jank and how do you find its cause?
qa.a: Jank is when frames miss their deadline, about 16 ms at 60 Hz, so the screen visibly stutters. I capture a system trace with Perfetto while reproducing it on a real device, find the long frames, and look at what the main thread was doing in those frames. That usually points to a specific slow function, such as image decoding or layout.

lessons.title: Memory and leaks
body: A leak happens when something long-lived (a singleton, a static field, a running coroutine or a listener) holds a reference to something short-lived, such as an Activity, View or Fragment. The garbage collector cannot free it.

Detect leaks with **LeakCanary** in debug builds and the Memory Profiler. Reduce memory pressure by sizing bitmaps to their view, using an image loader with caching (Coil or Glide), and responding to `onTrimMemory`.
points: Common leaks: static Context, listeners, inner classes, bindings
Avoid allocations in onDraw and hot loops
lessons.tip: When asked how you found a leak, describe the LeakCanary trace: the reference chain from a GC root to the leaked Activity.

code.title: A classic leak and its fix

p: Each app gets a limited heap, often a few hundred MB on modern phones and much less on cheap ones. The garbage collector frees objects that nothing references anymore. If your app keeps references to objects it no longer needs, memory grows until the app slows down from constant garbage collection or crashes with `OutOfMemoryError`.

A leak is a chain of references from something long-lived (a singleton, a static field, a running thread) to something short-lived (an Activity). The Activity is closed, but the chain keeps it, plus all its views and bitmaps, in memory. Rotate the phone a few times and you have several dead Activities stuck in memory.

code.title: Leaking with an inner class

p: Add LeakCanary as a `debugImplementation` dependency. It watches destroyed Activities, Fragments and ViewModels. If one is not freed after a few seconds, it dumps the heap and shows the exact reference chain. You fix the leak by breaking the link closest to the long-lived object.

mistakes.bad: Registering listeners without unregistering them
mistakes.good: Pair every register with an unregister in the opposite lifecycle callback.

mistakes.bad: Keeping big bitmaps in a static cache
mistakes.good: Use an image loader with a size-limited LRU memory cache.

mistakes.bad: Ignoring LeakCanary warnings as "debug only"
mistakes.good: The same leaks happen in release; fix them.

qa.q: How would you find and fix a memory leak?
qa.a: I would use LeakCanary in debug builds, or take a heap dump in the Memory Profiler after leaving the screen. LeakCanary shows the reference chain from a GC root to the leaked object. I fix it by breaking the reference at its source: unregistering a listener, clearing a binding, using applicationContext in a singleton, or stopping a callback in onStop.

lessons.title: Battery, network and app size
body: Batch and defer background work with WorkManager and constraints (charging, unmetered network). Avoid wake locks and frequent polling; use push messages (FCM) instead.

Network efficiency means fewer, smaller requests: compress responses, cache, paginate and prefetch only what is likely to be needed. App size affects install conversion; ship App Bundles, enable R8 and resource shrinking, and use WebP or vector images.
points: App Bundles and R8 for size
lessons.tip: Android vitals in the Play Console (ANR rate, crash rate, excessive wake-ups) is the production view interviewers expect a senior engineer to watch.

code.title: Deferring work to good conditions
code.src:
val upload = PeriodicWorkRequestBuilder<PhotoBackupWorker>(12, TimeUnit.HOURS)
    .setConstraints(
        Constraints(
            requiredNetworkType = NetworkType.UNMETERED,
            requiresCharging = true,
            requiresBatteryNotLow = true
        )
    )
    .build()
WorkManager.getInstance(ctx)
    .enqueueUniquePeriodicWork("photo-backup", ExistingPeriodicWorkPolicy.KEEP, upload)

p: The biggest costs are keeping the CPU awake (wake locks, frequent background work), using the radio (every network request wakes it up and it stays on for a while afterwards), and GPS. Small, frequent requests are worse than one larger batched request, because each one wakes the radio again.

Use WorkManager with constraints, such as unmetered network or charging, for work that can wait. Use push messages from the server (FCM) instead of polling every few minutes. Batch analytics events and send them together. Android's **Doze** mode and **App Standby Buckets** will limit apps that wake up too often anyway.

Ask for only what you need: paginate lists, request smaller image sizes, enable gzip, and cache responses. For app size, upload App Bundles, enable R8 and resource shrinking, use vector drawables or WebP, and check the **APK Analyzer** to see what takes space.

code.title: Batching analytics instead of sending each event

mistakes.bad: Polling the server every minute for updates
mistakes.good: Use FCM to tell the app when something changed.

mistakes.bad: Holding a wake lock "just in case"
mistakes.good: Use WorkManager; it manages wake locks for you.

mistakes.bad: Downloading full-resolution images for thumbnails
mistakes.good: Request the size you display.

qa.q: Why is sending many small network requests bad for battery?
qa.a: Each request wakes the cellular radio into a high-power state, and the radio stays in that state for several seconds after the request finishes before it powers down. Many small requests keep the radio awake much longer than one batched request carrying the same data, so batching saves a lot of battery.

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Behavioural rounds decide many offers, especially for senior roles. Interviewers want evidence of how you work: ownership, collaboration, handling conflict and failure, and the impact you had.
Prepare 6 to 8 real stories from your work and reuse them across questions. One story can show ownership, a technical decision and a lesson learned.
lessons.tip: Write your stories down before the interview. Under pressure, people forget their best examples.

code.title: A story bank template
code.src:
Story: Cut checkout crash rate
Situation : Checkout crashes at 1.8% after a payment SDK upgrade, peak sale in 2 weeks
Task      : I owned the fix as the payments module owner
Action    : Reproduced with a release build, found an R8 rule missing for SDK models,
            added a keep rule + a release smoke test in CI, coordinated with QA
Result    : Crash rate 1.8% -> 0.1%; no checkout incidents during the sale
Reuse for : ownership, debugging, working under pressure, process improvement

deep.h: What the interviewer is really checking
p: Behind every behavioural question are a few simple questions: Can this person own a problem? Do they work well with others? Do they learn from mistakes? Will they make the team better? Your stories should answer these, even if the question does not ask them directly.

Write down 6 to 8 real situations from your work: a hard bug you fixed, a project you led, a disagreement, a failure, a time you helped a teammate, a time you improved a process, a tight deadline. For each, note the numbers (crash rate, time saved, users affected). Then map each story to the questions it can answer.

Teams do great work together, but the interviewer is hiring you. Say "we" for the team's goal, and "I" for what you personally decided and did. It is not bragging; it is giving them the information they need.

code.title: Mapping stories to questions
code.src:
Question type             -> Best story
Tell me about a challenge -> Checkout crash during sale week
A time you disagreed      -> Compose migration plan
A failure                 -> Migration that lost drafts
Leadership / mentoring    -> Onboarding two juniors to Hilt
Tight deadline            -> Shipping UPI payments in 3 weeks
Improving a process       -> Adding release smoke tests in CI

mistakes.bad: Inventing stories on the spot
mistakes.good: Prepare real stories beforehand and practise them aloud.

mistakes.bad: Only saying "we did"
mistakes.good: Explain your own decisions and actions.

mistakes.bad: Giving answers without any result
mistakes.good: End with a measurable outcome or a clear lesson.

qa.q: Tell me about yourself. How should you structure this answer?
qa.a: Keep it to about 90 seconds: who you are now (role, platform, years), two or three highlights with impact, for example a performance win or a feature at scale, and why this role is a good next step. It is a guided summary that sets up the stories you want them to ask about, not your full CV.

lessons.title: The STAR method
body: Structure each answer as **Situation**, **Task**, **Action**, **Result**. Spend most of the time on Action (what *you* did and why) and finish with a measurable Result and what you learned.
Keep answers to about two minutes. Let the interviewer ask follow-up questions instead of covering every detail up front.
points: Reflection: what you would do differently
lessons.tip: End with the result, not the action. Many candidates stop at "and then I shipped it".

code.title: A STAR answer in short form
code.src:
Q: Tell me about a time you improved performance.

S: Our feed scrolled at ~40 fps on low-end devices; reviews mentioned lag.
T: I was asked to fix it before the next release.
A: Profiled with Perfetto, found image decoding on the main thread and full
   list refreshes. Moved to Coil with sized requests and replaced
   notifyDataSetChanged with ListAdapter + DiffUtil. Added a Macrobenchmark.
R: Jank frames dropped from 18% to 3%; the benchmark now runs in CI.

p: **Situation**: one or two sentences of context so the listener understands the stakes. **Task**: what you were responsible for. **Action**: what you did, in order, and why you chose that path. **Result**: what happened, ideally with numbers, plus what you learned.

A common mistake is spending a minute on background and ten seconds on what you did. Aim for roughly 15% Situation and Task, 60% Action, 25% Result and reflection. In the Action part, mention options you considered and why you picked one; that shows judgement.

code.title: A strong answer about a hard bug
code.src:
S: Payments failed for ~3% of users after a release, during a festival sale.
T: I was on call and owned the payments module.
A: Checked Crashlytics: all failures on Android 8 devices. Reproduced on an
   emulator, found an R8 rule missing for a new SDK model. Rolled back the
   staged rollout first to stop the damage, then shipped a hotfix with the
   keep rule and added a minified-build smoke test to CI.
R: Failures back to 0.1% within 6 hours. The CI check has caught two similar
   issues since. Lesson: always test the minified build before release.

deep.h: Keep it short, then go deeper on request
p: Aim for about two minutes. The interviewer will ask follow-ups on what interests them. That conversation often matters more than the first answer, so leave room for it.

mistakes.bad: Rambling through the whole project history
mistakes.good: Give just enough context, then move to your actions.

mistakes.bad: Results with no numbers
mistakes.good: Estimate if needed: "about 40% faster", "from 2% to 0.1%".

mistakes.bad: Skipping what you learned
mistakes.good: End with one honest lesson.

qa.q: Why do interviewers ask for specific past examples instead of hypothetical ones?
qa.a: Past behaviour is the best predictor of future behaviour. Hypothetical answers show what someone thinks they would do, while a real example shows what they actually did under real constraints, and follow-up questions can test the details. That is why STAR answers with concrete numbers are more convincing.

lessons.title: Conflict, feedback and collaboration
body: Expect questions such as "tell me about a disagreement with a teammate or manager". Show that you disagreed on the problem, not the person, used data to decide, and committed to the outcome even when it was not your proposal.
For feedback questions, give a real example of feedback you received, what you changed, and how you know it worked.
points: Disagree on ideas with data, then commit
Show empathy for the other side
Working with product, design and backend
lessons.tip: Never make the other person the villain. Interviewers are checking whether you are someone they want on their team.

code.title: Structure for a disagreement answer
code.src:
1. The disagreement:  Compose rewrite now vs incremental migration
2. Their view:        Faster in the long run, cleaner code
3. My view:           Risk to the Q3 launch, team not yet trained
4. How we decided:    Built one screen both ways, measured effort and bugs
5. Outcome:           Incremental migration, new screens in Compose
6. What I learned:    Prototype early instead of arguing in meetings

p: Interviewers want to see that you can disagree without damaging relationships. Show that you understood the other side, used data or a small experiment instead of opinions, and accepted the final decision even if it was not yours.

For feedback you received: what was said, how you felt honestly, what you changed, and how you know it helped. For feedback you gave: how you made it specific and kind, and focused on the work, not the person.

code.title: Feedback you received
code.src:
Feedback: "Your PRs are too large to review; reviews take days."
Reaction: Felt defensive at first, then checked: average PR was 1,200 lines.
Change:   Split work into stacked PRs under 300 lines, added a short
          "what to look at" note to each description.
Result:   Review time dropped from ~3 days to under 1; fewer bugs slipped through.

p: Android engineers work with product managers, designers, backend engineers and QA. Good stories show you pushing back on a design that would hurt performance, agreeing an API contract early with backend, or helping QA reproduce a bug quickly.

mistakes.bad: Describing a colleague as difficult or wrong
mistakes.good: Describe the disagreement neutrally and focus on how it was resolved.

mistakes.bad: A story where you were simply right and won
mistakes.good: Show listening, compromise and commitment.

mistakes.bad: Feedback stories with no change
mistakes.good: Explain what you did differently afterwards.

qa.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager.
qa.a: A good answer names the disagreement clearly, for example timeline versus quality, explains the manager's reasons fairly, shows how you raised your concern privately with data, and what was decided. If your view lost, say you committed fully and what you learned; if it won, show you did not make it about winning.

lessons.title: Ownership, failure and leadership
body: A failure question tests self-awareness. Pick a real mistake with real consequences, own your part plainly, and spend most of the answer on what you changed afterwards: a process, a test, a habit.
Senior roles add leadership without authority: mentoring, driving a technical decision across teams, improving engineering practices, and making trade-offs between speed and quality.
lessons.tip: Avoid fake failures like "I work too hard". They signal a lack of self-awareness.

code.title: Turning a failure into a strong answer
code.src:
Mistake : Shipped a migration that wiped local drafts for ~2% of users
Owned   : I wrote the migration and skipped testing from an older schema
Fixed   : Hotfix within 6 hours, restored drafts from server copies
Changed : Added MigrationTestHelper tests for every historic version,
          added a staged rollout rule for DB changes
Lesson  : Test the upgrade paths users actually have, not just the latest

p: Pick a mistake that mattered, that was clearly at least partly yours, and that taught you something lasting. It should not be a disaster that questions your basic judgement, and it should not be a fake failure. Most of the answer should be about what you changed afterwards.

Ownership means acting like the outcome is yours even when no one told you to: noticing a rising crash rate and fixing it, writing the missing documentation, improving the release checklist. These stories are especially valued for senior roles.

You do not need a manager title. Mentoring juniors, leading a technical decision across teams, writing a design doc others follow, or raising code quality through reviews are all leadership. Show how you influenced people and what changed because of it.

code.title: A leadership story outline
code.src:
Goal:     Move the app from 3 different networking stacks to one
My role:  Wrote a design doc comparing options; ran a 30-min review with 3 teams
Approach: Migrated one feature as a reference, paired with each team on theirs
Pushback: One team worried about deadlines -> agreed a later date for them
Result:   One stack in 2 quarters; 18% less networking code; fewer auth bugs

mistakes.bad: Blaming others in a failure story
mistakes.good: Own your part clearly, even if others contributed.

mistakes.bad: Fake weaknesses like "I care too much"
mistakes.good: Pick a real weakness and show how you manage it.

mistakes.bad: Leadership stories that are just "I told them what to do"
mistakes.good: Show how you persuaded and supported people.

qa.q: What is your biggest weakness?
qa.a: Name a real but manageable weakness relevant to work, for example taking on too much myself instead of delegating. Give a quick example of when it caused a problem, then explain the concrete system you now use to manage it, such as breaking work into tasks others can pick up, and the result. It shows self-awareness and growth.

lessons.title: Questions to ask and closing
body: At the end you will be asked whether you have questions. Ask about the team's real problems: how they ship, how they measure quality, what the first 90 days look like, and what success means in this role.
Use your last minute to connect your experience to their needs in one or two sentences.
points: Ask about the team, product and engineering practices
Ask what success looks like in 3 to 6 months
Avoid salary questions in technical rounds
Close with a short fit summary
lessons.tip: Questions about their release process and quality metrics show you think like an owner, not only an implementer.

code.title: Good questions to ask
code.src:
- What does a typical release look like, from PR to Play Store rollout?
- How do you measure app quality today (crash rate, ANRs, performance)?
- What is the biggest technical challenge the Android team faces this year?
- What would make someone very successful in this role in six months?
- How are architecture decisions made and documented?

deep.h: Your questions are part of the interview
p: "Do you have any questions?" is your chance to learn whether you want the job, and it shows how you think. Questions about engineering practice, quality and real challenges signal that you will act like an owner.

How releases work and how often they ship. How they measure quality (crash rate, ANRs, performance). The biggest technical challenge this year. How decisions are made and documented. What success looks like in the first months. How the Android team works with backend and design.

In the last minute, briefly connect your experience to what you heard. For example: "You mentioned startup time is a priority; I cut startup by 40% at my last company using Baseline Profiles and lazy SDK init, so I would love to help with that."

code.title: After the interview
code.src:
Same day:  Short thank-you message (2-3 lines), mention one topic you enjoyed
Notes:     Write down questions you were asked and where you were unsure
Next time: Turn weak answers into prepared stories

mistakes.bad: Saying "No questions"
mistakes.good: Prepare at least three questions for each round.

mistakes.bad: Asking things the website already answers
mistakes.good: Ask about how the team actually works.

mistakes.bad: Discussing salary in an early technical round
mistakes.good: Save compensation for the recruiter or HR conversation.

qa.q: What questions would you ask at the end of an Android interview?
qa.a: I would ask how a release goes from pull request to full rollout, how they track app quality such as crash rate, ANRs and startup time, what the biggest challenge for the Android team is this year, and what would make someone successful in this role after six months. These show I care about shipping quality software, not just writing code.

lessons.title: Introduction
body: Mobile system design asks you to design an app or SDK end to end in 45 to 60 minutes: requirements, architecture, data flow, offline behaviour, APIs and trade-offs. There is no single right answer; interviewers grade your reasoning and communication.
Mobile rounds differ from backend ones: they focus on the client (caching, sync, battery, flaky networks, app size and lifecycle), with the backend treated mostly as an API.
lessons.tip: Say the time plan out loud at the start. It shows structure and lets the interviewer steer you to what they care about.

code.title: A 45-minute plan
code.src:
0-5 min   Clarify: features in scope, users, scale, offline needs, platforms
5-15 min  High-level design: screens, modules, layers, data flow diagram
15-30 min Deep dive: data model, API, caching, pagination, sync, errors
30-40 min Non-functional: performance, battery, security, testing, monitoring
40-45 min Trade-offs, what you would do next, questions

p: There is no single correct design. Interviewers look at how you clarify requirements, structure the problem, choose sensible components, explain trade-offs and react to new constraints. Thinking out loud is essential: a silent good design scores lower than a reasoned average one.

Backend design is about servers and scaling to millions of requests. Mobile design is about one device with limits: unreliable networks, limited battery and memory, the app being killed at any time, slow app updates and many device types. Your design should show you handle those well.

1) Requirements. 2) High-level architecture. 3) Data model and API. 4) Deep dive into one or two hard parts (pagination, sync, caching, real-time). 5) Non-functional concerns: performance, offline, security, testing, monitoring. 6) Trade-offs and what you would improve.

code.title: Questions to ask in the first five minutes
code.src:
- Which features are in scope? (feed, posting, likes, comments?)
- How many users, and how large is the content? (images, video?)
- Must it work offline? Read only, or also writes?
- Real-time updates needed? How fresh must data be?
- Which Android versions and devices? Tablets?
- Any limits: app size, battery, data usage?

mistakes.bad: Jumping straight into classes and libraries
mistakes.good: Clarify requirements and scope first.

mistakes.bad: Designing the backend in detail
mistakes.good: Treat the backend as an API unless asked; focus on the client.

mistakes.bad: Staying silent while thinking
mistakes.good: Talk through your reasoning and options.

qa.q: How do you start a mobile system design interview?
qa.a: I spend the first few minutes asking clarifying questions: which features are in scope, expected scale, offline needs, real-time needs and device constraints. Then I summarise the agreed scope and share my plan for the time, such as high-level design first, then deep dives into the hardest parts, so the interviewer can steer me.

lessons.title: Requirements and API design
body: Split requirements into **functional** (what the app does) and **non-functional** (latency, offline, battery, security, scale). Confirm scope before designing; it is fine to say which features you will leave out.
Design the API contract the app needs: endpoints or GraphQL queries, cursor-based pagination, error formats, and whether to use polling, push notifications, SSE or WebSockets for real-time updates.
lessons.tip: Cursor pagination does not skip or duplicate items when new posts arrive. Explain why offset pagination fails for feeds.

code.title: A feed API contract
code.src:
GET /v1/feed?cursor=eyJpZCI6...&limit=20
200 {
  "items": [{ "id": "p_91", "author": {...}, "media": [...], "createdAt": 1729420000 }],
  "nextCursor": "eyJpZCI6InBfNzIifQ",
  "hasMore": true
}

POST /v1/posts/p_91/like
Idempotency-Key: 7f9c-...      # safe to retry on flaky networks

p: **Functional**: what the user can do, such as "see a feed", "like a post", "send a message". **Non-functional**: how well it must work, such as "opens in under 2 seconds", "works offline", "messages arrive within a second". Non-functional requirements usually drive the interesting design decisions.

List the endpoints the app needs and their shape. Use **cursor-based pagination** for feeds: the server returns a cursor that marks where the page ended, and you send it to get the next page. Offset pagination (`page=3`) breaks when new items are added, causing duplicates or missed items.

code.title: Sending a message safely

p: **Polling**: simple, but wasteful and slow to update. **Long polling**: the server holds the request until there is news. **Server-Sent Events**: a one-way stream from server to app. **WebSocket**: two-way and low latency, best for chat, but you must handle reconnects. **FCM push**: wakes the app when it is in the background.

mistakes.bad: Using page numbers for an infinite feed
mistakes.good: Use cursors so new posts do not cause duplicates.

mistakes.bad: Retrying POST requests without idempotency
mistakes.good: Send an idempotency key so duplicates are ignored.

mistakes.bad: Choosing WebSockets for everything
mistakes.good: Use them only where real-time two-way traffic is needed.

qa.q: Why is cursor-based pagination better than offset pagination for a feed?
qa.a: With offset pagination, if new posts are added at the top while the user scrolls, every item shifts down and the next page repeats items the user already saw, or skips some on deletion. A cursor marks an exact position, such as the last item's ID and timestamp, so the next page always continues from the right place.

lessons.title: Client architecture
body: Describe the layers: UI (Compose screens + ViewModels), domain (optional use cases) and data (repositories over a local database and the network). The database is the single source of truth and the UI observes it.
Name the key components: image loader, pagination (Paging 3 with RemoteMediator), background sync (WorkManager), push (FCM), analytics and a feature-flag layer.
lessons.tip: Draw the arrow API → database → UI, never API → UI. It is the one diagram every mobile design answer should have.

code.title: Data flow for a paged feed

p: Start with boxes: UI (screens and ViewModels), domain (optional use cases), data (repositories), local storage (Room), remote (Retrofit API, WebSocket), background work (WorkManager), and shared services (image loader, analytics, auth). Draw arrows for how data moves. Interviewers love a clear diagram.

The key arrow is **network → database → UI**. The UI observes the database, the repository refreshes it from the network, and background jobs sync changes. This one decision handles offline mode, rotation, process death and consistency all at once.

code.title: A feed architecture in text
code.src:
FeedScreen (Compose)
   ↑ state            ↓ events
FeedViewModel  --  collects Flow<PagingData<Post>>
   ↓
FeedRepository
   ├── Pager + RemoteMediator ──► FeedApi (Retrofit, cursor pages)
   └── PostDao (Room) ◄── writes pages, UI reads from here
ImageLoader (Coil: memory + disk cache)
SyncWorker (WorkManager): likes/comments outbox

p: A `PagingSource` loads pages from one place (for example the database). A `RemoteMediator` fetches new pages from the network when the database runs out and saves them into the database. The `Pager` connects them and exposes a `Flow<PagingData>` that lists in Compose or RecyclerView consume, loading more as the user scrolls.

mistakes.bad: UI reading straight from the network
mistakes.good: Route network data through the database.

mistakes.bad: Listing libraries without explaining roles
mistakes.good: Explain what each box is responsible for.

mistakes.bad: Forgetting images in a feed design
mistakes.good: Discuss image sizes, caching and prefetching.

qa.q: Why route network data through the local database instead of showing it directly?
qa.a: It gives one source of truth, so every screen shows the same data. The app works offline and survives process death without refetching. Updates from any source, such as refresh, sync or user edits, flow to the UI automatically, and it makes pagination and caching simpler with tools like Paging's RemoteMediator.

lessons.title: Offline, sync and real time
body: Decide what must work offline: reading cached content, composing actions (likes, messages) that are queued and sent later. Store pending actions in an outbox table and send them with WorkManager, using idempotency keys so retries are safe.
For real-time features (chat, live location), use a WebSocket while the app is in the foreground, FCM to wake the app for important events, and a sync-on-open fallback to catch up on anything missed.
points: WebSocket in foreground, FCM in background
Catch-up sync with a last-seen cursor
lessons.tip: Mention what happens when the server rejects a queued action. Interviewers often probe the unhappy path.

code.title: Optimistic like with an outbox

p: When the user likes a post, show the like instantly instead of waiting for the server. Save the change locally, update the UI, and send it in the background. If the server rejects it, roll back and tell the user. This makes the app feel fast even on slow networks.

A sync has two directions. **Push**: send local pending changes (the outbox) to the server, oldest first, with idempotency keys. **Pull**: ask the server for everything changed since your last sync token and write it into the database. Run sync on app open, when the network returns, and on a schedule with WorkManager.

code.title: Pull changes since the last token

deep.h: Real-time in the foreground and background
p: For chat, keep a WebSocket open while the app is visible and reconnect with backoff when it drops. In the background, rely on FCM high-priority messages to notify the user. When the app opens again, run a catch-up sync from the last known message, in case some events were missed.

mistakes.bad: Keeping a WebSocket open in the background
mistakes.good: Close it when the app is hidden; use FCM in the background.

mistakes.bad: No plan for rejected optimistic updates
mistakes.good: Roll back the local change and show a clear message.

mistakes.bad: Syncing everything from scratch every time
mistakes.good: Use a sync token to fetch only changes.

qa.q: How would you make sure no chat messages are lost if the WebSocket disconnects?
qa.a: Every message has a server sequence number or timestamp, and the app stores the last one it received. On reconnect, or when the app opens, it asks the server for all messages after that point before resuming the live stream. Outgoing messages sit in a local outbox with client IDs and idempotency keys until the server confirms them.

lessons.title: Non-functional concerns and trade-offs
body: Cover performance (startup, scroll, image sizes), battery (batching, constraints), security (token storage, pinning, no secrets in the app), observability (crash reporting, analytics, performance monitoring) and rollout (feature flags, staged releases).
Close by naming trade-offs explicitly: what you chose, what you gave up and when you would choose differently. That is what separates senior answers.
lessons.tip: Practise with Droidly's system design walkthroughs below. Do each one out loud with a timer.

code.title: Stating a trade-off clearly
code.src:
Decision : WebSocket for chat while the app is open
Gain     : Sub-second delivery, typing indicators
Cost     : Battery and connection handling; must reconnect with backoff
Fallback : FCM data messages when backgrounded + sync on open
Revisit  : If most users are on poor networks, consider long polling

p: **Performance**: image sizes, list efficiency, startup. **Battery and data**: batching, constraints, caching. **Security**: token storage, HTTPS, pinning, no secrets in the app. **Reliability**: retries, offline, process death. **Observability**: crash reporting, logs, performance traces, analytics. **Release safety**: feature flags, staged rollouts, kill switches.

deep.h: Scaling the app and the team
p: As the app grows: split it into feature modules, keep shared design system components, add remote config for quick changes without a release, and set up CI with tests and benchmarks. Mentioning these shows you think beyond the first version.

For each big choice, say what you gain, what it costs, and when you would choose differently. For example: a WebSocket gives instant messages but costs battery and reconnection complexity; polling is simpler but slower. Interviewers remember candidates who name the costs of their own choices.

code.title: Wrapping up in the last five minutes
code.src:
1. Recap the design in 3 sentences
2. Name the riskiest part and how you would de-risk it
3. List what you would measure after launch (crash rate, feed load p90, sync success)
4. Mention the next improvements (prefetching, smarter caching, offline posting)

mistakes.bad: Ending without a summary
mistakes.good: Recap the design and the key trade-offs.

mistakes.bad: Ignoring monitoring and rollout
mistakes.good: Explain how you would know it works in production.

mistakes.bad: Claiming the design has no downsides
mistakes.good: Name the costs and when you would change your choice.

qa.q: How would you know your feed design works well after launch?
qa.a: I would track client metrics: time to first feed content, scroll jank and frame time, image load times, error and retry rates per endpoint, crash and ANR rates, and how often users see stale or empty states. I would roll out behind a feature flag in stages and compare these metrics against the old version before going to 100%.
